entries.what: Minimal networked note-taking with backlinks, daily notes and end-to-end encryption, plus an AI assistant over your own notes.
entries.priceDetail: $10/month. Free trial, no free tier.
notes: End-to-end encryption is the distinguishing feature — the option if someone here keeps notes on client work they would rather not have sitting in plaintext.
Rated Low: $10/month with no free tier for a notes app, against Hejour and Obsidian doing much of it for less.

entries.name: Heptabase
entries.what: Visual knowledge base — notes as cards on an infinite whiteboard, so a subject can be laid out spatially and then linked into a structure.
entries.priceDetail: $8.99/month billed annually, $17.99/month monthly, with a $53.99/month team tier. Free trial, no free tier.
notes: The spatial approach genuinely suits research and discovery work — laying out everything known about a client's problem before writing it up.
Rated Low: single-purpose and paid-only. Worth it for someone who thinks visually, wasted on everyone else.

entries.name: Aqua Voice
entries.what: Dictation for Mac, Windows and iPhone aimed at AI workflows — speech to formatted text with editing by voice, and a mode for dictating into prompts.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier. Paid at $8/month and $24/month, with $12/user/month for teams.
notes: The direct alternative to Wispr Flow at half the price, and explicitly built for dictating prompts to agents — which is the use that actually saves time here.
Try both on a week of real prompting. The difference is cleanup quality, and it is a matter of preference.

entries.name: Goblin Tools
entries.what: Small free tools that break an overwhelming task into steps, estimate effort, and adjust the tone of a message — built with neurodivergent users in mind.
entries.priceDetail: Free on the web; a small one-off charge for the mobile apps.
notes: The Magic ToDo breaks a vague task into steps at whatever granularity you ask for — genuinely useful on the days a job feels too big to start.
Free, no account, no product roadmap trying to become a platform. Rare and worth keeping a link to.

entries.name: Delphi
entries.what: Builds a queryable agent from one person's body of work — books, podcast episodes, lectures, posts and threads — so their audience can ask questions and get answers in their voice, with the sources behind each one.
entries.priceDetail: Free $0 tier. Paid at $79/month and $299/month.
notes: This is the answer to a request we get and should not build: a consultant, author or coach wanting to 'clone my expertise'. Pointing them at $79/month beats quoting a bespoke retrieval product that will need maintaining forever.

Their own homepage runs Lawrence Lessig — 12 books, 84 podcast episodes, 62 lectures, 210 posts — which is a real implementation at real scale rather than a mock-up, and worth showing a sceptical client.
It is the client's own likeness and voice being reproduced, so the consent and accuracy questions are theirs to own. Put that in writing before we recommend it into a brand.

entries.name: Vellum
entries.what: Personal AI assistant with a persistent machine behind it — each plan buys real vCPU, memory and storage, so it holds long-running context, works in Slack and on mobile, and has an email address of its own. Open source and self-hostable.
entries.priceDetail: Free to start. Mighty $30/month (1 vCPU, 2GiB, 10GB, $25 credits included). Super $100/month (2.5 vCPU, 5GiB, 30GB, $45 credits). Ultra $200/month (4 vCPU, 8GiB, 60GB, $115 credits). Self-hosting available.
notes: Read this before recommending it to anyone: Vellum used to be an LLM development and evaluation platform, and that is what most developers still think it is. It has pivoted entirely to a personal assistant, so old bookmarks, tutorials and comparisons describe a product that no longer exists here.
Open source and self-hostable is the genuine differentiator against Halo — an always-on assistant holding studio context that can run on our own infrastructure rather than someone else's.
Priced as compute rather than seats, with credits on top, so the real monthly cost depends on usage. Rated Low until someone has run it for a month and knows what it actually costs.

entries.name: awesome-ios-design-md
entries.takeaway: Reverse-engineered design systems for 200 real apps as plain markdown — exact brand hexes, full type ramps, component states, spacing grids, motion curves and haptics — in four flavours each: framework-neutral, SwiftUI, Expo and Jetpack Compose. Hand one to a coding agent and it stops inventing the styling. MIT, by Muhammed Eliwat.
entries.whatToDo: Already done: all 200 apps and 800 specs are vendored into this site under /design-md, with the licence alongside, so they survive the repo going quiet. Action: on the next app build, open the closest app's spec and take the structure — the spacing grid, the motion curves, the component states — not the brand colours.
entries.cost: Free. MIT licence on the documents; the brands they describe are not licensed to anyone.
notes: The specs are unusually good: not "use a card with a shadow" but the actual hex, the actual type weight ladder, the actual spring curve and haptic. That is the difference between an agent producing something plausible and something that looks native.

The IP line matters more here than anywhere else on this site. These are other companies' trade dress. Lifting Bumble's yellow and hexagons into a client's dating app is not inspiration, and the proprietary typefaces named throughout — Brando, Uber Move, Airbnb Cereal, Spotify Mix — must be licensed separately. Take the mechanics; leave the identity.
One maintainer, and the value is entirely in the documents rather than in any service, which is exactly why they are copied into our repo rather than linked.

entries.name: Spectr gallery
entries.takeaway: Live browser-rendered previews of every screen in the 200 apps that awesome-ios-design-md documents, so you can see the interface a spec describes before reading 25KB of markdown. The same outfit sells generating a DESIGN.md from your own screen recording.
entries.whatToDo: Use it as the visual index to the specs on /design-md — find the screen, then take the spec. Action: when a client references "something like the Spotify now-playing screen", open it here on the call rather than describing it.
entries.cost: Gallery is free to browse. Generating your own spec from a recording is their paid product; figures not checked.
notes: The pairing is the point: the gallery shows what a screen looks like, the spec says why. Neither is much use to an agent without the other.

Their generate-from-a-recording product is the interesting bit for us — a client's existing app turned into a spec our agents can build against. Unpriced here, so treat it as worth a look rather than a plan.

entries.name: Kitbitz
entries.what: 2,000+ hand-drawn illustrations across 13 themed Figma kits — built as reusable components with colour variables and smart resizing, so a scene can be recoloured and rescaled rather than redrawn. SVG and PNG download, a Figma plugin for browsing and inserting, and an MCP endpoint so an agent can pull assets directly.
entries.priceDetail: Free under CC0 — public domain, commercial use included, no attribution required.
notes: CC0 is the headline. Every other illustration set on this list carries a licence to read before shipping — unDraw asks nothing but is not public domain, Storyset's terms would not even render, Thiings prices by the client's revenue. This one has no strings at all, which makes it the safe default for client work.
Components with colour variables rather than flat SVGs means a set can be pulled into a client's palette in one change, which is the usual failure of free illustration.
A year of one person's work on a game product that did not launch, released rather than binned. Hand-drawn, so it has a house style — check it suits the brand before committing a whole site to it.

entries.name: Forge (UI8)
entries.what: Free macOS app that opens a local web project as a visual canvas — arrange and edit the real thing rather than a mockup of it. Files stay on disk in your repo, ready to commit, so there is no export step and no second source of truth.
entries.priceDetail: Free macOS app, per its own description. No pricing page published.
notes: "Your work always lives on disk, in your repo" is the part that matters and the part every design-to-code tool on this list gets wrong. Nothing to export, nothing to reconcile, no Figma file drifting from the build.

sticky.ui8.dev is their demo of what it can do — a 3D sticker toy on Three.js and WebGPU. Worth opening for the capability, but its own page renders client-side and served us nothing, so it is not listed separately.

The site is a single-page app and served only its own title and description, so the app was assessed from that rather than from a feature list. macOS only. Download it before promising anything on a client project.

entries.name: Spherium
entries.what: WebGL globe and map generator in the browser — pick a projection and region, choose the point shape (triangle, hex, matrix, line), set density up to 8k points, adjust graticules and opacity, then export the result as SVG.
entries.priceDetail: No pricing, account or paywall published anywhere on the site; it runs in the browser and exports directly. Marked Beta 1.0.
notes: Vector export is what makes it useful rather than a toy: the dotted-globe hero that appears on every infrastructure and fintech site, as an SVG we can recolour and animate, instead of a stock PNG or an afternoon in Illustrator.
Density up to 8,000 points will make a heavy SVG. Check the file size before it goes into a page we are also promising to keep fast.
Beta, no pricing published, single maintainer. Export what you need and keep the file — do not design a client page around the tool staying up.

entries.name: Bible Strong Avatar Lab
entries.what: Procedural 2D avatar studio in the browser — build a character from parts, set expressions and animations, then export it as reusable React, JavaScript, SVG or PNG rather than as a flat image.
entries.priceDetail: No pricing, account or paywall published anywhere on the site.
notes: The React and JavaScript export is the difference from every other avatar generator: the output is a component that can take props, so a client's app can render an avatar per user rather than shipping a folder of PNGs.
Procedural and animated covers the empty states, onboarding and loading moments that otherwise get a stock illustration or nothing.

A side project attached to a Bible study app, which is an odd provenance for a design tool and worth knowing before it goes in a client's dependency list. The export is code we own, so the risk is limited to the editor disappearing.

entries.name: hunk
entries.what: Terminal diff viewer built for reviewing agent-authored changesets — a multi-file review stream rather than a per-file pager, with inline AI annotations, watch mode, exact-line agent guidance, 64 themes, TypeScript extensions and Git, Jujutsu and Sapling support. Ships agent skills alongside the binary.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source, MIT. `npm i -g hunkdiff`, or an install script. v0.19.0 at the time of adding, 8.6k GitHub stars.
notes: This is the answer to the actual daily problem with coding agents: a 40-file diff that is technically correct and unreviewable. A review-first stream across files beats `git diff | less` and beats scrolling a pull request in a browser.

Second option alongside meat, already on this list — meat abridges a diff into a conceptual summary, hunk keeps every line but makes the review navigable. Different jobs; try both on the same agent changeset.

The bundled agent skills and live session control are the interesting half: the reviewer can hand exact-line guidance back to the agent rather than you retyping it. MIT, so there is no vendor to outlive.

entries.name: Frontpages
entries.takeaway: A curated gallery of landing page front pages — hero sections from across the web, searchable by category and company, updated weekly. Its author pitches it as a free version of Mobbin for the web rather than for apps.
entries.whatToDo: Reference at the start of a marketing site. Action: pull ten hero sections in the client's category before wireframing, so the structure argument happens against shipped examples rather than opinions.
entries.cost: Free. Optional email subscription for the weekly update.
notes: Narrower and more useful than a general inspiration gallery: it indexes the one section every client argues about most, and it is free where Mobbin's web coverage is behind $10/month.
Hero sections only, so it complements Saaspo's section-level index rather than replacing it.
Other companies' pages. Structure and hierarchy are the input; the styling is theirs.

entries.name: IP as Logo
entries.summary: Generates simple, cute mascot logos that still read at 32×32 — three directions, then six candidates for approval.
entries.description:
An **Agent Skill** for generating company-ready IP mascots: one dominant silhouette from 4–7 basic shapes, exactly two character colours plus one solid background, thick rounded forms, and a large character emerging from the lower-left or lower-right.

It is opinionated about process, not just style. The agent inspects the repo for product context first, asks one consolidated round of questions if that is not enough, proposes three directions, and only generates after you agree — six candidates, split evenly between lower-left and lower-right so each direction is tested from both sides.

Written to the open Agent Skills format, so it works with any compatible agent rather than one product. Install with `npx skills@latest add s1dashu/ip-as-logo-skill`.
entries.promptText:
---
name: ip-as-logo
description: Generate extremely simple, cute, personified square character images with rounded heavy forms, two purposeful character colors, one solid background color, and a dominant lower-corner composition. Use when creating an animal, creature, robot, ghost, plant, object, or other character image, including when the agent should infer three product-relevant directions and propose six independent candidates for approval.
---

# IP as Logo

Create the simplest possible cute IP character: a compact, lovable symbol that remains recognizable at `32 × 32`, not a detailed character illustration.

## Workflow

1. Parse the request for an explicit IP subject and available product context. Do not ask the user to choose a color mode unless they explicitly want to control it.
2. When the user has not specified an IP subject and the current workspace is a product repository, inspect relevant read-only context before asking questions. Prefer the README, product docs, package or app metadata, landing-page copy, manifests, and design tokens. Treat context as sufficient when the product purpose, primary audience, and intended personality can be inferred with reasonable confidence.
3. When product context is insufficient, ask one consolidated round of background questions covering what the product does, who it serves, and how it should feel. Do not start a second background questionnaire. Continue with the best supported interpretation after the answer.
4. Once context is sufficient, always present three concise directions before generation and explicitly propose generating six independent candidates in one batch. Do not generate until the user agrees, unless the current request already explicitly authorizes six outputs or asks the agent to proceed without another confirmation.
5. Choose the three proposed directions deliberately:
   - When the user explicitly specifies an IP subject, keep that subject and propose three distinct design treatments based on silhouette treatment, secondary color region, defining feature, or personality emphasis.
   - When the user does not specify an IP subject, propose three genuinely different IP subjects or metaphors. Tie each one to a different product attribute or brand promise; do not return three arbitrary animals with no rationale.
6. Interpret the user's response exactly:
   - If the user accepts all three directions and the six-image proposal, generate two independent variants per direction and label them `A1`, `A2`, `B1`, `B2`, `C1`, and `C2`. Assign `A1`, `B1`, and `C1` to the lower-left and `A2`, `B2`, and `C2` to the lower-right so every direction is tested once from each side.
   - If the user selects one direction but accepts six images, generate six controlled variants of that direction and label them `A1` through `A6`. Assign odd-numbered variants to the lower-left and even-numbered variants to the lower-right.
   - If the user rejects the proposed quantity, directions, or distribution, follow the user's replacement instructions without arguing for the default.
   - For any other even default batch size, split candidates equally between lower-left and lower-right. For an odd batch, assign the extra candidate to either side deliberately and record the imbalance. Do not use bottom-center unless the user explicitly requests it.
7. Default every candidate to exactly three semantic colors in the complete image: exactly two IP base colors plus exactly one background color. Reuse the two IP colors for facial marks rather than introducing additional semantic colors. Follow an explicit user request for another color count. Keep required product cues, identifying features, complexity limits, and any supplied palette consistent enough for useful comparison.
8. Determine the available image-generation path before promising output. In Codex, use ImageGen when it is available. In any other agent environment, use an available configured image generator; if none is available, ask the user whether they can provide or enable one. Do not fabricate generated results.
9. If the runtime supports subagents, parallelize the six independent candidates up to the available concurrency. Give every subagent the same product brief, shared constraints, and one assigned direction or variant; run remaining candidates in subsequent waves when capacity is limited. If subagents are unavailable, generate the candidates through separate image-generation calls or jobs.
10. If the user supplies a background palette, reserve every supplied color for backgrounds unless they explicitly say otherwise. Choose exactly two IP base colors independently for the subject and context unless the user also assigns subject colors. Do not treat any historical or example palette as a closed list of allowed backgrounds.
11. Abstract each subject using the complexity budget below. Generate every candidate as a separate full-resolution square asset; never ask an image model to compose a contact sheet, grid, or multi-image sheet. Do not use previous candidates as image references when testing prompt-only reproducibility.
12. Treat each batch as a one-pass creative draw. Generate every requested candidate once, then preserve and deliver every returned result as-is. Do not inspect outputs to block delivery, classify them as recommended or non-recommended, retry them automatically, or repair them with post-processing.
13. Preserve and label every generated result. Report every label, IP direction and rationale, assigned corner, saved path, prompt/color mapping, and dimensions. Present all results together; generate refinements or replacements only when the user explicitly asks for another draw.

When proposing directions before generation, describe each in one compact line: `<IP subject> — <product connection> — <defining silhouette>`. End with a direct proposal to generate six images using the distribution above. Do not turn the discovery phase into a long branding workshop unless the user asks for one.

## Complexity budget

- Build one dominant continuous outer silhouette from roughly `4–7` large basic geometric shapes. Merge or delete any shape that does not carry identity, expression, or recognition.
- Use at most one species-defining feature: for example, one large pouch beak, one pair of curled horns, or one broad visor.
- Use at most two broad internal color regions corresponding to the two IP base colors. Keep the face to two eyes and, only when needed for the expression, one tiny mouth. Omit eyebrows, highlights, nostrils, texture, outlines, and decorative marks unless essential for recognition.
- Remove repeated feathers, scales, fur tufts, armor plates, buttons, screws, numbers, labels, and other illustrative detail.
- Make simplification, cuteness, and an endearing baby-like personality the decisive qualities. Favor a large head, compact proportions, soft cheeks, widely spaced simple eyes, and a calm friendly expression when appropriate to the subject.
- Require a readable black silhouette and recognizability at `32 × 32`. If a feature disappears or becomes noise at that size, enlarge, merge, or remove it.

## Shape language and composition

- Use thick, rounded, weighty contours and broad color masses.
- Forbid sharp corners, pointed ears or beaks, needle-like tails, thin antennae, thin smiles, narrow gaps, and acute flame or feather tips. Replace every necessary tip with a visibly blunt rounded end.
- Show both members of paired identifying features, such as ears, horns, wings, gills, or bells.
- Show the character upright and emerging from the assigned lower-left or lower-right corner, filling about `85–95%` of the canvas so the IP remains visually dominant.
- Cropping at the bottom or assigned side is welcome when it strengthens the sense of emerging from that corner, but do not prescribe exact edge contact or a fixed crop.
- Never center or bottom-center the character unless the user explicitly requests it.
- Preserve both members of paired identifying features within the visible composition.
- Keep the artwork upright; never rotate the canvas or tilt the main mark without an explicit request.

## Simplicity and visual treatment

- Start from large, clean semantic shapes and the strongest possible simple silhouette. The character should be understood immediately, before any internal feature is noticed.
- Prefer fewer, larger, softer forms over extra definition. Do not add a feature merely to explain anatomy or material.
- Keep facial marks tiny, simple, and subordinate. Do not add glossy hotspots or detailed cavity rendering to eyes, mouths, noses, or other small features.
- Keep the named background color visually solid and uniform, without scenery, texture, halo, vignette, or lighting variation.
- Ask for the subtle dimensional effect only with the single sentence used in the Prompt skeleton. Do not expand it into numerical strength or instructions for gradients, highlights, or shadows. Incidental gradients, shading, or mild dimensionality returned by the generator are acceptable and must not trigger filtering or retrying.
- Keep the requested visual direction graphic and simple rather than asking for clay, inflatable, plastic, plush, toy-like, or photorealistic rendering.

## Color and canvas

- Default to exactly three semantic colors in the complete image: exactly two IP base colors plus exactly one background color.
- Choose the two IP colors from the product context, subject identity, intended personality, and user request. Organize both into broad purposeful masses; reuse one for facial marks and keep the other in one continuous defining region rather than scattering decorative fragments.
- Choose both subject colors independently from the background. Favor clear, lively subject colors when appropriate, but do not impose global saturation, OKLCH, hue-shift, or chroma bands on the IP.
- Choose the background freely for the context or from a user-supplied palette. Unless the user asks for vivid color, gently mute the background by lowering its saturation a little; keep it clearly chromatic and intentional rather than vivid, gray, or muddy. Historical palettes and examples are suggestions only, never an allowlist or mandatory default palette.
- Preserve clear visual separation between the dominant IP silhouette, its facial marks, and the background. If a user-supplied background causes weak separation, adjust the subject colors first rather than replacing the requested background.
- Across a batch, vary the two-IP-color strategies deliberately instead of repeating the same neutral-heavy combination.
- Treat the two character colors as semantic color families. Incidental tonal variation within either family does not invalidate an output.
- Name the intended solid background color directly. Ask for it to fill every open area and the unoccupied corners while the assigned emergence corner is occupied by the character. Do not use image-mode terms such as `opaque`, `alpha`, or `transparency` in the generation prompt.
- Generate a direct `1:1` square with square outer corners. Request approximately `1536 × 1536`; accept and preserve a native `1254 × 1254` result when that is the service output limit. Never resample merely to reach the requested number.

## Prompt skeleton

### Route constraints by generator capability

Determine the available image model and its actual tool schema from runtime metadata, configured provider documentation, or an explicit user statement. Do not guess a model or invent unsupported parameters.

Describe the requested visual as an image only. Never tell the image generator that the image is a `logo`, `brand mark`, `app icon`, `icon asset`, or intended for any of those uses. Do not prepend use-case or asset-type scaffolding that reveals such a use. This rule applies only to the generation prompt; the surrounding user conversation and Skill name may still describe the broader project.

- For modern instruction-following image models such as GPT Image 2, Nano Banana Pro, and Seedream 5.0 Pro, keep the complete positive prompt and express the minimal exclusions as the natural-language `Constraints:` line inside the main prompt. Do not create a separate negative-prompt payload for these models.
- For an older model or runtime that explicitly exposes a dedicated parameter such as `negative_prompt`, keep every positive prompt line unchanged and deliver the minimal exclusions through that dedicated parameter in the syntax required by the available adapter. Omit the natural-language `Constraints:` line from the main prompt to avoid duplicating the same exclusions in both channels.
- For an older model without a dedicated negative-prompt parameter, follow its documented prompt format. When only one prompt string is available, retain the concise natural-language `Constraints:` line.
- Record the model or provider, the detected constraint-delivery mode (`main-prompt constraints` or `dedicated negative parameter`), and the exact constraint text or payload in the generation report.

When a dedicated legacy negative-prompt parameter is available, adapt this minimal payload to its required syntax:

```text
text, watermark, borders, frames, cards, presentation masks, extra subjects, scenery, thin fragile lines, sharp tips, photorealistic materials, strong three-dimensional rendering, external cast shadows
```

For modern instruction-following models and single-prompt interfaces, use the following complete prompt:

```text
Create one complete full-bleed 1:1 square image.
Background: fill the entire square with solid <background>. Keep <background> visible in every open area and in the corners not occupied by the character; the assigned emergence corner must be occupied by the character.
Subject: place one extremely simplified, cute, endearing <subject> IP character on the background, reduced to one soft rounded continuous silhouette and one defining feature.
Complexity: use only 4–7 large basic shapes and at most two broad internal color regions. Use two simple eyes and add one tiny mouth only when it helps the expression. Remove every nonessential line, outline, anatomical detail, texture, and decoration. Keep the character readable at 32 × 32.
Color behavior: use exactly three semantic colors in the complete image: exactly two IP base colors plus the background color. Choose the two IP colors from the subject and context, organize both into broad purposeful masses, and reuse them for facial marks. Choose the background independently or follow the user's supplied background. Unless the user asks for vivid color, lower the background saturation slightly so it feels gently muted and restrained while remaining clearly chromatic, clean, and intentional rather than gray or muddy. Keep the IP, facial marks, and background clearly separated. Treat any example palette as optional inspiration, never as an allowlist.
Composition: keep the character upright and emerging from the assigned <lower-left or lower-right>, filling about 85–95% of the square so it remains visually dominant. Cropping at the bottom or assigned side is welcome when it strengthens the corner emergence. Preserve both paired identifying features. Never center or bottom-center the character.
Style: make simplification, cuteness, and lovable baby-like appeal the strongest qualities. Use large soft forms, compact proportions, thick rounded contours, and an ultra-clean graphic treatment. Prefer one clear shape over several explanatory details. Add an extremely, extremely subtle, almost imperceptible sense of depth through a barely-there neo-skeuomorphic treatment.
Finish: show only the character on the full-canvas background, with clean surfaces and normal square outer corners.
Constraints: Use no text or watermark. Add no borders, frames, cards, or presentation masks. Include one character only, with no extra subjects or scenery. Use no fragile lines, sharp tips, unnecessary outlines, tiny details, or decorative marks. Add no photorealistic material, dramatic bevel, glossy hotspot, deep occlusion, extrusion, strong three-dimensional rendering, or external cast shadow. Keep the background solid and uniform, with no texture, vignette, or lighting variation.
```

## Delivery behavior

- Treat generation as a stochastic draw, not a conformance test.
- Generate the requested number of independent candidates once and deliver every returned image.
- Do not inspect or report alpha, transparency, or background mode by default.
- Do not block delivery, rank candidates as compliant or non-compliant, mark them as recommended or non-recommended, or automatically retry any result because of its background, colors, detail, composition, gradient, shading, or dimensionality.
- Do not post-process a result to make it appear more compliant. If the user later requests another direction or replacement, generate a new independent candidate in response to that explicit request.
whatYouGet: A full SKILL.md with the workflow, the complexity limits and the colour rules
A three-directions-then-six-candidates approval loop rather than one-shot generation
Explicit guidance to keep the mark legible at 32×32
Image-only generation prompts that never mention logo or app-icon use, which is what stops a model producing a mockup instead of a mark
install: npx skills@latest add s1dashu/ip-as-logo-skill
Add --global for a personal install available across projects
Needs an image generator available in the agent — ImageGen in Codex, or any configured generator elsewhere

entries.name: Agentation
entries.what: Dev-only React overlay that turns a click on any element of your running app into context an agent can act on: CSS selector, source file path, React component tree, computed styles and your note, copied out as markdown — or read straight from the browser by its MCP server, so Claude Code can list annotations, discuss them and mark them resolved.
entries.priceDetail: Free. `npm install agentation -D`, v3.0.2 at the time of adding. No pricing page. Licensed PolyForm Shield 1.0.0 — source-available with a non-compete, not open source.
notes: This closes the worst gap in agent work, which is saying where the problem is. Instead of "the blue button in the sidebar" the agent gets `.sidebar > button.primary` and a file path it can grep. React 18 and Next.js, which is what we ship.

There is a Claude Code route as well as copy-paste: `npx skills add benjitaylor/agentation`, then `/agentation` detects the framework, installs the package and wires the provider into the layout. With the MCP server the paste step goes entirely — "fix annotation 3" — and it exposes tools like `agentation_resolve` so the annotation disappears from the browser when the agent has dealt with it.

Read the licence before it goes anywhere near a handover: PolyForm Shield is not MIT. Dev-only by design behind a NODE_ENV guard, and desktop only — there is no annotating on a phone, which is where half of client feedback comes from. Built by Benji Taylor, Dennis Jin and Alex Vanderzon; no data leaves the browser.

entries.name: Svelte Agentation
entries.what: Svelte port of Agentation's annotate-and-paste loop: mount it in development, press `i`, click an element, write a note, copy structured markdown for Claude Code or Cursor. Its inspector pierces open shadow roots, so elements inside web components annotate like anything else on the page.
entries.priceDetail: Free, MIT. `pnpm add sv-agentation`. v0.4.0 on npm, nine releases since March 2026 — the site still advertises v0.3.0.
notes: Only reach for this on a Svelte job; for our React work the original at agentation.dev is the one to install. It earns a listing as the pattern proven in a second framework, and for the shadow-DOM piercing, which the original does not claim.

It depends on `element-source`, published by the same author with no licence field at all and untouched since March 2026. MIT on the wrapper does not cover an unlicensed dependency — that is a real gap if it ever goes near client code.
Single maintainer (Sikandar Bhide), and the docs already lag the package by a version.

entries.name: Svelte Shadcn Blocks
entries.what: Marketing and UI blocks for shadcn-svelte — heroes, pricing, logo clouds, testimonials, footers, auth — installed with the jsrepo CLI, plus an MCP server so Cursor or Windsurf can pull a block in without a browser. A Svelte port of Méschac Irung's cnblocks.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source, MIT.
notes: Svelte only, and a port rather than the source, so it trails cnblocks upstream. On a React job go to the original Tailwind blocks instead.

The transferable idea is the MCP server sitting in front of a component library: the agent asks for a pricing block and gets the real source, rather than inventing one. Worth copying for our own Foundry components.
Its own counts disagree — the page says 150+ blocks while the og:title still says 50+ — so verify what is actually there before promising a client a library.

entries.name: Svelte QBlocks
entries.what: shadcn-svelte blocks organised by primitive with a variant count against each — accordion 4, alert dialog 2, avatars 14 — so you choose a variant rather than a component, with preview and source side by side.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source. No npm package; the source is on GitHub and the site is the catalogue.
notes: Svelte only. The organising idea is the useful part: a count beside every primitive shows immediately where a library has depth and where it has one token example — most catalogues hide that.
Lives on a vercel.app subdomain with no custom domain and a single maintainer, so treat the URL as temporary and take a copy of anything we actually use.

entries.name: Svelte Dot Matrix
entries.what: Dot-matrix loaders for Svelte 5 in TypeScript and Tailwind — Hex Orbit, Braille Beat, Lemniscate Pulse, Radar Arc, Binary Bloom — each a named grid animation with a setup guide and copy-paste source.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source. The index lists 69 named loaders against the site's own "50+" claim.
notes: The components are Svelte, but a dot-matrix loader is a grid and a keyframe schedule — the timing and the shape of each one read straight across to a React or CSS implementation. Useful as a catalogue of loader ideas even if none of the code ships.
Sixty-nine variations on a spinner is more than any project needs; the value is picking two that suit a brand, not adopting the set.

entries.name: Svelte Efferd Blocks
entries.what: Thirty categories of shadcn-svelte page blocks — hero, header, logo cloud, features, integrations, testimonials, CTA, pricing, blog, auth, app shell, FAQ, contact, footer, image gallery — each with a preview/code toggle and a tree-style source explorer, installed through the shadcn-svelte registry.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source. Installed with `pnpm dlx shadcn-svelte@latest add`, on Cloudflare Pages.
notes: The install command on the live site is broken: the copy button on /blocks/image-gallery serves `pnpm dlx shadcn-svelte@latest add http://sveltekit-prerender/r/image-gallery-one.json`, with SvelteKit's prerender placeholder host left in place of the real origin. Anyone following the docs gets a fetch error, and it tells you how much of this is checked after deploy.
Svelte only. The tree-style source explorer is the part worth stealing — seeing a block's file layout, not just its markup, is what makes a copy-paste library usable.

entries.name: Svelte Datatables Examples
entries.what: Worked examples of TanStack Table v9 in Svelte — filtering, sorting, pagination — split into filter components, documentation and whole table blocks rather than one kitchen-sink demo.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source.
notes: The most portable of this family, because TanStack Table v9's core is framework-agnostic: the column definitions, filter state and pagination wiring are the same objects we would write in React, only the rendering layer differs. Read it as v9 documentation with better examples than the official ones.
Svelte adapter code will not paste into a React project, and v9 is newer than the v8 most of our tables would be on, so check which major a client project is pinned to before copying anything.

entries.name: Svelte Animations
entries.what: 50+ animated components and effects for Svelte 5 built on Motion SV — ports of the Magic UI, Spell UI and Fancy Components sets — with a CLI install and a command palette for finding them.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source.
notes: Ports of React libraries into Svelte, so for us the originals are the destination — Magic UI in particular. Listed for the Svelte case and because the port makes a decent map of which Magic UI effects people actually reach for.

The real find underneath is Motion SV (`motion-sv`, MIT, by HanielU), the Svelte binding for Motion that all of this animates with. That is the dependency to note if a Svelte job ever needs real motion.

entries.name: IP as Logo library
entries.takeaway: The companion gallery to the IP as Logo skill already in the starter library: a searchable wall of finished mascots made with it, each downloadable as its original PNG, with favourites and six UI languages. The skill's README states every logo is free for commercial use. Built as a Supabase and Cloudflare R2 front end, so it is a real library rather than a screenshot of one.
entries.whatToDo: Source. Action: pull two or three mascots as stand-in brand marks for Foundry pitch decks and early prototypes rather than generating from scratch, and run the skill itself (`npx skills@latest add s1dashu/ip-as-logo-skill`) when a client needs something of their own.
notes: Not a client identity. Every visitor can download the same mascots, so treat this as placeholder and side-project material — the skill is what produces something a client can own.
PNG only: the download is the original raster, with no SVG, so anything that needs to scale or recolour has to be redrawn.
The commercial-use grant is a line in the GitHub README (MIT, s1dashu, 2026), not a licence file on the site itself. Keep a copy of that wording if a logo ever ends up in front of a client.
Single maintainer, a client-side app on Supabase with the publishable key in the bundle and assets on cdn.ipaslogo.com. Fine for what it is; download anything we rely on rather than hotlinking it.

entries.name: Claude Academy
entries.takeaway: Anthropic's own course catalogue: 289 courses, tutorials and use cases in one filterable list. The ones that matter to us are Claude Code 101 (12 lessons on what it is and the core workflows), Claude Code in Action (9 lessons on long hands-off sessions — plan mode, steering compaction, the rewind menu, autonomous loops, verification), Introduction to agent skills (6 lessons from a first skill to team distribution), Claude subagents (4 lessons on orchestrating them deterministically), Introduction to MCP, Introduction to Claude Cowork (14 lessons) and Building with the Claude API (67 lessons covering tool use, RAG, agents and production patterns).
entries.whatToDo: Training. Action: everyone does Claude Code in Action and Introduction to agent skills — they are an hour each and they cover exactly the things people are currently guessing at, from compaction to skill distribution. Then Building with the Claude API for whoever is next on an agent build.
entries.note: Start here. Everything else on this site assumes you already know what Claude Code can do.
notes: This is the answer to most of the "how do I make it stop doing that" questions: plan mode, directing compaction so a summary keeps what matters, rewinding a session, when to hand over to a loop. All of it documented by the people who built it rather than inferred from a thread.
Courses open without an account — "Start course" works, and signing in only saves progress and completion badges. Free, © 2026 Anthropic PBC, and the catalogue is filterable by product.

Most of the 289 entries are not for us: the AI Fluency family (builders, educators, nonprofits, small businesses, students, pK–12) and the Bedrock and Vertex courses are 65-plus lessons each. Filter to the Claude Code and skills material and ignore the rest until there is a reason.

entries.name: Beautiful UI
entries.what: Twenty copy-paste React primitives for the parts of an agent interface nobody has a pattern for yet: loading and thinking states with expandable traces, streaming text with inline sources and follow-ups, human-in-the-loop approval cards, tool-call chips, live task rows, diff and filter tables, and a full agent screen.
entries.priceDetail: Free to copy. No accounts, no package — the components are lifted out of the site. Built by Turbo, a product design studio, as a shop window for their own work.
notes: This is the vocabulary we keep reinventing on every agent build — what a thinking state looks like, how a tool call reads, where the approval sits. Having twenty of them drawn properly is worth more than any component library of buttons.

Copy-paste means no version to upgrade and no vendor to outlive, but it also means no fixes arrive: whatever we take becomes ours to maintain. Check each one against our own tokens rather than pasting the studio's styling.

entries.name: Generative Loaders
entries.what: React loading states for generative interfaces: sixteen animated text reveals (decode, typewriter, cascade, redact, line-by-line, dissolve), eighteen compact inline activity indicators, and twelve image-generation placeholders. One npm package, accessible by design.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source, MIT. `npm install generative-loaders`, React 18 and newer.
notes: The waiting state is most of an AI interface's perceived quality, and it is the bit that always gets a spinner. Sixteen text reveals with a live gallery to pick from saves an afternoon per project.
Single maintainer (Kasturi Khanke), CI on the repo, docs and an issue template — tidier than most. Bundle it rather than adopting the whole thing if only two of the forty-six get used.

entries.name: Is Agentic
entries.what: Scores how much of a website an AI agent can actually discover, retrieve, understand and use, then hands back the evidence. `npx is-agentic [domain]`. Essential checks carry the weight — server-rendered content, correct HTTP behaviour, document structure, recoverable errors, usable controls — and API, OAuth, GraphQL, MCP or commerce checks only activate when a scan finds those surfaces.
entries.priceDetail: Free to scan, run from the CLI or the site. Scans are run by Ora; the site publishes a rolling leaderboard, which is worth knowing before pointing it at a client domain.
notes: This is the audit we have been describing to clients without a number attached. It is also a sales tool: netflix.com scores 43 and salesforce.com 46 on their own leaderboard, which is a conversation opener with anyone who thinks their site is modern.
Checks that do not apply are excluded rather than failed, so a brochure site is not punished for having no API — that is the detail that makes the score usable on client work.
Public leaderboard: it rotates recent scores hourly. Scan a staging domain if a client would object to their score appearing on someone else's homepage.

entries.name: deepsec
entries.what: Agent-powered vulnerability scanner from Vercel Labs that you run in your own infrastructure, aimed at on-demand review of every file in a large existing repo. `npx deepsec init`. Work fans out across worker machines, and an interrupted run resumes by skipping the files it already analysed.
entries.priceDetail: Apache-2.0, free to install — the cost is the model usage. Their own README says a large codebase can run to thousands or tens of thousands of dollars, tunable with `--thinking-level`.
notes: Worth knowing exists, and worth reaching for once on a project we have inherited and cannot read. It is configured for the best models at maximum thinking, which is why it finds things a linter never will and why the bill is what it is.
Read the cost warning as written, not as marketing modesty: this is not a tool to point at a repo casually. Scope it to a directory and set the thinking level before anyone runs it.
Vercel Labs, Apache-2.0, resumable — the engineering around it is sound. The judgement call is entirely about spend.

entries.name: CodeBurn
entries.what: Works out where AI coding spend actually goes across 41 providers and shows it three ways: `npx codeburn` in the terminal, `npx codeburn web` for a dashboard, and `codeburn menubar` for a macOS menu bar or Windows tray readout.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source, MIT, on npm as `codeburn`. 11k GitHub stars and 816 forks at the time of adding. Sponsorship funds keeping the integrations current.
notes: We have no idea what a given client project costs us in agent time, and the provider dashboards do not add up across four accounts. Forty-one integrations in one readout is exactly the missing number.

Its own pages disagree on the count: the README talks about keeping 41 integrations honest while the repo's social card says 37 tools and agents. Either way it is more than any single provider dashboard, but treat the figures it reports as a working estimate until they have been checked against one real month's invoice.

entries.name: Boop
entries.what: A self-hosted notification inbox for developers: POST a JSON event from any server and it arrives on your phone. One Go binary, one SQLite file, one Docker container, pushing straight to Apple's APNs — no hosted relay, no account system, no telemetry.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source, MIT — 737 GitHub stars, 35 forks and three contributors at the time of adding. Go server plus an iOS app; you run the server and pair it with your own APNs credentials.
notes: The right shape for build alerts, deploy notices and cron failures on client infrastructure: the events never leave our own boxes, which is the objection every hosted alerting service runs into on a client audit.
Self-hosting is the price — an APNs key, a container and a certificate to remember. Fine for Foundry, harder to hand to a client as a supported thing.

entries.name: Matte
entries.what: Native macOS recorder and editor for product demos: capture the iOS simulator, a live device or any app window, then add device frames, backgrounds, animations and captions and export. Version 2.0, in open beta, adds full 3D.
entries.priceDetail: 2.0 beta is free with no account, macOS 15+. Pro is $10/mo, $39/yr (about $3.25 a month) or $149 one-time, each covering 4K export, no watermark and up to three Macs, with a 15-day money-back window.
notes: App Store screenshots and client demo videos are a recurring half-day. This is the tool that turns that into twenty minutes, and the frames and backgrounds are good enough to ship without a designer touching them.
$149 once for three Macs is the version to buy if it survives a first project; the beta is free and needs no account, so it can be tried on real work first.

entries.name: Ditther
entries.what: Browser image and video effects editor with 75+ stackable effects — dither, halftone, ASCII, pixel and voxel, distortion, print, retro, colour and light — over layers, text and shapes, with animation for motion output.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier covers the core effects, 1080p video and 100+ backgrounds. Pro $8/mo (down from $15), or Pro+ lifetime $69 one-time (down from $139), for all effects, saved custom looks and weekly background drops.
notes: The fastest route to the dithered, halftoned, ASCII look that keeps turning up in brand work, without setting up a shader pipeline. Free tier is enough to know within ten minutes whether it earns the $69.
In-browser and stackable means it is a playground rather than a repeatable pipeline: nothing here is version-controlled, so treat the output as an asset and keep the source file.

entries.name: Ultramock
entries.what: Turns product screens into presentation visuals: customisable videos, still visuals and 3D mockups of UI, websites and apps.
entries.priceDetail: Its own pitch says free; the Design Minis listing has it as freemium, and the pricing page is client-rendered so no figure could be read from a static fetch.
notes: Pitch decks and case studies need a screen in a frame on a background, and doing it by hand in Figma is an hour we bill to nobody.
The pricing page would not render for a static read, so what a paid tier costs is unverified — check before anyone builds a deck around it.

entries.name: Reelfolio
entries.what: Turns a folder of screenshots, mockups and screen recordings into a portfolio showreel: 263+ shot styles with the cinematography, timing and polish pre-designed, backgrounds and framing controls, and cloud rendering to 16:9, 1:1, 9:16 and 4K.
entries.priceDetail: One-time purchase per its own homepage; the figure is on a client-rendered pricing page and could not be read from a static fetch. Found via the Design Minis listing, which has it as paid.
notes: A case-study reel from a folder of screenshots, with no After Effects and no timeline, is worth having the week before a pitch.
Templated cinematography looks templated at volume — good for a portfolio piece, wrong for anything that has to carry a client's brand.
The URL Dan sent was the Design Minis listing rather than the product; reelfolio.com is a blank page, the real site is reelfolio.io.

entries.name: Amicons
entries.what: 760 hand-drawn icons in 3,040 variants — two fills and two styles each, on a 24px grid with a 2px stroke — organised into 43 categories, shipped as Figma and optimised SVG.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier is 300 icons and 1,200 variants with no updates. Pro is priced by company size and paid once: $89 for one person, $199 up to 10 staff, $449 up to 50, $899 up to 250, $1,799 up to 1,000, then enterprise.
notes: A warmer alternative to Phosphor and Lucide when a product needs personality without going illustrative, and four variants per icon covers dark UI and data-dense dashboards from one set.
The licence is per company size, so a Gitwork licence at $199 does not cover a client's own team — worth pricing into a project rather than discovering later.

entries.name: Libraries.dev
entries.what: Jakub Antalik's collection of React effect libraries under one roof — Gooey (`liquid-gooey`), where touching elements merge and morph like jelly while text stays crisp, plus Border beam, Thinking orbs, Metal and Image — each with a playground, install instructions and a copyable prompt.
entries.priceDetail: Free to install from npm; a Pro tier and a Studio for tuning sit behind sign-in, with no figure published on the pages read.
notes: Gooey is the liquid-metal merge effect everyone has been asking for since Apple shipped it, done as SVG filters over real DOM so text and images stay sharp.
The URL Dan sent (gooey.jakubantalik.com) is now just a redirect notice — the product moved to libraries.dev, and the npm package name is unchanged.

entries.name: COBE
entries.what: A 5KB WebGL globe with no dependencies: markers, arcs and any DOM element bound to a point on the surface, so CSS transitions, filters and interactivity work on labels and stickers. v2 adds satellites, flights, live badges and analytics overlays.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source, MIT. `npm i cobe`, works with React, Vue, Svelte or vanilla.
notes: The spinning globe is a landing-page cliché precisely because it works, and this is the version that does not cost 500KB of three.js to get.
By Shu Ding at Vercel, MIT, zero dependencies — about as safe as a client-work dependency gets.

entries.name: ShipSwift (SwiftUI library)
entries.what: AI-native SwiftUI component library: production-ready components plus an MCP server and a skills repo, so an agent can be handed the whole set and build a real iOS app against it. Demo app on the App Store, iOS 18+, Swift 5+.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source, MIT. Installed as a Swift package; the MCP server is how an agent reads it.
notes: The interesting part is the shape, not the components: a component library with an MCP server in front of it, so the agent gets real source instead of inventing SwiftUI. Worth copying for our own Foundry components.

The URL Dan sent (shipswift.app) is the marketing site for Signer Labs, an agency selling custom builds at $5K for four weeks — the library is the open-source half of a funnel. Listed here as the library, which is the part we would actually use.

entries.name: genart (Claude Code plugin)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin that teaches the working knowledge of long-form generative art: seeding a PRNG from a token hash, rendering the same composition at any resolution, trait and rarity design, preview capture signalling, and export for print and pen plotters. Covers Canvas 2D, p5.js, three.js/WebGL and SVG, and ships runnable tools.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source, MIT, versioned as a Claude Code plugin with CI on the repo.
notes: Deterministic hash-seeded rendering is the whole craft of generative work and it is the bit an agent gets wrong unaided. This is also the closest thing to a worked example of a plugin that teaches a discipline rather than wrapping a tool.
Aimed at onchain platforms — Art Blocks, 256ART, Verse, Highlight, Plottables — so parts of it are irrelevant to us. The seeding, resolution-independence and plotter export are the transferable half.

entries.name: watermarks-remover
entries.what: Agent skill plus a standard-library Python service that strips multi-vendor AI provenance marks — invisible characters and metadata — from text and files. The skill is a thin client that drives the service.
entries.priceDetail: Free and open source, MIT, with CI and tagged releases.
notes: The real use for us is hygiene: model output carries zero-width characters and metadata that break diffs, CMS fields and copy-paste into client systems. This strips them in one pass.
Its own framing is content you own, and that is the line to hold — using it to pass model output off as hand-written is a different thing, and not something we would do on client work.

entries.name: VibeUI
entries.what: 92 layout prompts for AI UI generation across 15 categories — auth forms, pricing tables, hero sections, bento grids, nav, testimonials, dashboards, onboarding — each describing a structure to paste into a builder so it lays out the page rather than inventing one.
entries.priceDetail: Free to browse and copy. The site upsells GlowUp UI, a paid product from the same people, for generating variants across models.
notes: Structure prompts are the missing half of vibe coding: models default to one hero and one pricing table, and naming the layout is what breaks them out of it. Ninety-two of them, categorised, is a decent starting bank.
This is a prompt library, so it is ours to fork the moment it is useful — worth lifting the good ones into the Foundry starter library rather than depending on someone's marketing site.

entries.name: OGFolio
entries.what: A library of nearly 900 Open Graph images collected from real products, with an OG image analyser that checks a URL's dimensions, file size and meta tags. From the people behind Toolfolio.
entries.priceDetail: Free to browse; no pricing published on the pages read.
notes: The OG image is the one asset every client project needs and nobody designs — 900 real examples plus a checker is the fastest way to get one right rather than guessing at 1200×630.
Same stable as Toolfolio, already on the list, so expect the same directory-with-affiliate-links model.

entries.name: Grainient
entries.what: Around 1,450 background assets in one subscription: 375 grainy gradients, 450 smooth blends, 90 animated gradients and 538 AI-generated backgrounds, plus a shader tool for making your own.
entries.priceDetail: $149 a year (billed annually, about $13 a month) or $299 once for lifetime access, both including a commercial licence. No usable free tier — the collections are behind sign-in.
notes: Hero backgrounds are a recurring half-day of nudging blur and noise. A commercial licence across 1,450 of them at $299 once is cheaper than the time, and the shader tool covers the case where none of them fit.
Check the licence terms against client work specifically — a commercial licence held by us is not always a licence the client inherits when they take the site over.

entries.name: Codenotch
entries.what: Mac utility that parks your LLM usage in the notch: a running readout of what the coding agents have burned through, without opening a dashboard.
entries.priceDetail: Free. v1.5.0 at the time of adding, universal binary, macOS 26 and newer.
notes: The number that matters during a build is the one you can see without stopping, and the notch is dead space. Pair it with CodeBurn, which does the same job properly across 41 providers but needs a command.
macOS 26+ only, by a solo designer (@hivinz_), with no licence or source published — fine for a personal machine, not something to standardise on.

entries.name: BetterMouse
entries.what: macOS mouse utility meant to replace Logitech Options and friends: configurable smooth and discrete scrolling, cursor acceleration split from speed, per-button and per-gesture mapping to shortcuts and system actions, drag panning, and hardware settings for supported Logi mice including DPI, onboard profiles and thumbwheel.
entries.priceDetail: $7.99 one-time for life, with a 7-day full-functionality trial and five reusable activations per licence.
notes: Anyone on an MX Master and a Mac knows the Logi driver is 300MB of background processes to bind two buttons. This is the lightweight, privacy-safe replacement, and $7.99 once is not a decision.
Only worth it for a third-party mouse — on a trackpad it solves nothing.

entries.name: Imageory
entries.what: A personal gallery of AI images with the prompt that made each one, sorted into collections — gradients, landscapes, abstract, surreal, celestial, noise — so a prompt can be lifted rather than rewritten.
entries.priceDetail: Free to browse; an account saves favourites. No pricing published. Built by one person, Palak (@palakonweb).
notes: Prompt-with-image is the useful pairing — most galleries show the output and hide the recipe. Worth a look when a brief needs a texture or a background and nobody wants to spend an hour prompting.
The URL Dan sent was the signup page; this is the product. Small, personal and one maintainer, so treat it as a reference rather than a dependency.

entries.name: laurie
entries.what: Turns a laptop keyboard into a chord instrument: rich chords on keys 1–7, strumming on the trackpad, and live MIDI out to a DAW.
entries.priceDetail: Free to play in the browser; no pricing published, and the page is client-rendered so there is nothing else to read from it.
notes: No use on client work whatsoever. It is here because trackpad strumming into a DAW is a genuinely clever bit of interface design, and it takes ten seconds to try.
Everything beyond the pitch is behind client-side rendering — no platform notes, no licence, no team.

entries.name: Parafield AI
entries.what: Pitched as a personalised 3D sound experience for productivity, mindfulness and imagination. The site is a single client-rendered page and publishes nothing beyond that line — no product detail, no platform, no pricing, no team.
entries.priceDetail: Nothing published. Listed here as unassessed rather than assessed as good.
notes: Read and found to be a landing page with a tagline and no product behind it that could be verified. Kept on the list because Dan sent it, marked Unknown so nobody mistakes that for a recommendation.
Worth a second look if it ships something — as it stands there is nothing to judge.

entries.name: Interfaces
entries.takeaway: Jakub Krehel's design engineering magazine, issued rather than blogged: animation, typography, layout and colour worked through in depth, with live demos in the page — issue 12 is a typography manual for the web. His argument is that when anything can be replicated with a prompt, building fast stops being an advantage and only care shows.
entries.whatToDo: Reference. Action: read issue 12's typography manual against our own type scale, and put the interaction-detail pieces in front of whoever is next on a component build.
notes: The nearest thing to a curriculum for what we call design engineering, written by someone doing it rather than describing it.
Subscription-gated — the price is not published on the pages that render without an account, and /subscribe 404s to a static fetch.

entries.name: jmswrnr.com (James Warner)
entries.takeaway: A design engineer's site that doubles as a technique bank: nine 'artifacts' with working code — smooth circle pointer, floating hover cursor, React hex viewer, dynamic image contrast, image glitch shader, hero shader, one-time password input, draggable scroll area, 3D ASCII head — alongside write-ups on canvas-to-LED streaming, protecting Next.js API routes and building a 3D site header.
entries.whatToDo: Reference. Action: lift the one-time password input and the draggable scroll area next time either comes up, and read the shader artifacts before anyone writes a hero effect from scratch.
notes: Each artifact is a small, self-contained implementation rather than a tutorial, which is the useful format. No licence stated on the page, so ask before shipping his code verbatim.

entries.name: Design Minis
entries.takeaway: A directory of small tools made by designers, each doing one job properly — colour pickers, type scales, easing curves, shadow generators, dither and halftone effects — filterable by category, platform and price. Where Reelfolio, Ultramock and a dozen other one-job tools surface first.
entries.whatToDo: Source. Action: check it before building a one-off utility; the odds are it exists and is free.
notes: Submission-driven and sponsor-funded, so listings are what people sent rather than what is best — the filters do the work.
It carries an Easings cubic-bézier editor, which is the same job as the easing lab in our own experiments room.

entries.name: Sidebar
entries.takeaway: Five design links a weekday, chosen and tagged, running for over a decade. Typical day mixes a product-management essay, a typography piece, a small tool and a piece of criticism — the closest thing the field has to a daily paper.
entries.whatToDo: Reference. Action: put it in a shared channel rather than one person's inbox, so the good links reach the whole studio.
notes: One sponsored slot at the top each day, marked as such.

entries.name: SEESAW
entries.takeaway: Hand-picked web design inspiration updated daily, searchable by site, font or category — agency, AI, crypto, design tools, developer tools, fintech, portfolios, productivity. Each entry carries a one-line description of what the product does, so it reads as competitor research as much as inspiration.
entries.whatToDo: Source. Action: search it by category at the start of a client project rather than trawling Dribbble.
notes: Sponsor-funded with a newsletter attached. Overlaps Recent, Saaspo and Frontpages, already on the list — the difference is the font search and the descriptions.

entries.name: Inspora
entries.takeaway: A curated archive of recent visual and creative work, updated hourly, split into web, branding, product, motion, illustration, 3D and print. Broader than the site galleries — branding and print sit alongside interface work.
entries.whatToDo: Source. Action: use the branding and print cuts when a project needs identity references rather than UI ones, which the other galleries do not cover.
notes: Client-rendered, so the archive itself will not show up in a text scrape — it has to be browsed.

entries.name: Catalog
entries.takeaway: Studio Offgrid's library of design resources, sorted into apps, foundries, inspiration, mockups, publications, skills, studios and tools. The foundries and publications sections are the parts other directories do not have.
entries.whatToDo: Source. Action: use the foundries list when a project needs type beyond the usual free families, and the studios list as a reference for positioning work.
notes: Curated by one studio, so it reflects their taste rather than aiming at coverage. Client-rendered.

entries.name: local.ai
entries.takeaway: Independent benchmarks for running models locally, comparing intelligence, speed and energy use across Apple silicon and NVIDIA GPUs, with live data and an energy wall.
entries.whatToDo: Reference. Action: check it before quoting a client on on-device inference, and before anyone specs a Mac for local models.
notes: In early access, and the data tables are client-rendered — the figures could not be read from a static fetch, so treat the site as the source rather than anything quoted second-hand.
Energy use per token is the number nobody else publishes, and it is the one that decides whether local inference is actually cheaper.

entries.name: Creating Web Widgets Using the Document Picture-in-Picture API
entries.takeaway: Firefox 151 shipped the Document Picture-in-Picture API, so any HTML, CSS and JavaScript can now be put in a floating always-on-top window — tickers, live chat, playlists, to-do lists, notes. Daniel Schwarz walks through cloning a component into the window and the media queries and pseudo-classes for styling it, and makes the point that lifting a component out of its context breaks its CSS.
entries.whatToDo: Reference. Action: consider it for the next client dashboard that needs a always-visible readout, and read the CSS-context warning before anyone reuses a component in one.
notes: Published 27 August 2026. It is now in Firefox and Chromium, not Safari, so anything built on it needs a fallback for Mac users.

entries.name: 101 Ads
entries.takeaway: Every billboard on Highway 101 through the Bay Area, mapped and categorised, as a snapshot of what Silicon Valley is currently selling itself. The build is the interesting part: the author had Claude write an iOS app that used Vision to snap, crop and OCR billboards while he drove, then publish to the site, and vibe-coded the site itself.
entries.whatToDo: Reference. Action: read it as a worked example of an agent-built data pipeline — camera to OCR to published site with almost no manual input — and as a read on how the AI market is positioning itself.
notes: A personal project, refreshed roughly monthly by its author's own account. No use on client work; genuinely instructive about what one person plus an agent can assemble.

entries.name: Mike Barton (mikes.cv)
entries.takeaway: Portfolio of a multidisciplinary software designer in Manchester. Sent twice, so worth keeping as a reference point for how a UK design engineer positions and presents themselves.
entries.whatToDo: Reference. Action: use it as a benchmark when we next rewrite our own case studies — and as a name to know locally.
notes: The whole site is client-rendered: nothing beyond the name and the one-line description could be read from a static fetch, so the work itself has not been assessed here.

entries.name: The Twelve-Factor App
entries.takeaway: Twelve rules for building an app that can be deployed repeatedly without hand-holding, written by Adam Wiggins at Heroku in 2011 from watching a few hundred thousand apps rot. The ones that still catch people: config lives in the environment and never in the repo, dev and production are kept as alike as possible, logs are an unbuffered stream the app writes to stdout rather than files it manages, processes hold no state between requests, dependencies are declared explicitly rather than assumed present, and build, release and run are three separate stages so a deploy can be rolled back to an exact artefact.
entries.whatToDo: Reference and shared vocabulary. Action: use factors III (config), V (build/release/run), X (dev/prod parity) and XI (logs) as the checklist when taking on an inherited client app or handing one back, and check they line up with what Pulse already scans for.
notes: The text on the site has not been touched since 2017 and was written for Heroku dynos in 2011, so it predates containers as a default, Kubernetes, serverless and edge runtimes. Port binding (VII) and scaling via the process model (VIII) are Heroku assumptions rather than laws, and there is nothing in it about secrets management, observability beyond logs, or build caching.

Not abandoned though: it was open-sourced in late 2024 and a replacement is being written in the open at github.com/twelve-factor/twelve-factor under CC BY 4.0, with a Discord, a mailing list and posts through 2025. The site you would send someone to is nine years behind that work.

Value to us is as a checklist and a shared vocabulary for readiness and handover conversations, not as a methodology to follow literally. Copyright now sits with Salesforce; the manifesto text in the new repo is CC BY 4.0.

entries.name: Dive Radio
entries.takeaway: The landing page for a weekly live design show, built as a working vintage radio set. You drag a tuning dial through static to find 92.6 MHz and lock the signal; other frequencies hold hidden stations playing archive recordings. Behind it sits a Morse-timing mini-game called Byte Dial — four packets to intercept, tap on a solid light and hold on a hollow ring, scored perfect/clean/missed with a server-validated leaderboard and a prize draw. Roughly 80KB of vanilla JavaScript: no framework, no WebGL, no animation library.
entries.whatToDo: Reference for a launch or campaign page that has to earn attention rather than ask for it. Action: pull it apart before the next time a client asks for a teaser site, and note how little code the whole thing takes.
notes: The audio is the interesting part: static and the tuning sweep are synthesised live in Web Audio — buffer sources, a dozen gain nodes, two biquad filters, one oscillator, playback-rate bending — while the stations themselves are sampled. The same graph shape as a synth, used as set dressing.

Everything in it is a day or two of work each except the contest, which carries real weight: an API that validates tap timings server-side, entry forms, official rules and a draw. Copy the radio, not the sweepstake, unless someone is prepared to own the legal side.

The hidden stations lean on historical recordings. NASA audio and anything pre-1930 is almost certainly clear, but not everything of that kind is, so a version of this would need the provenance checked per clip rather than assumed.
No licence and no repo — it is a product site, so it is reference for how it is made, not something to lift from.

entries.name: Arc UI
entries.what: 157 React components and 91 composed blocks with the motion already in them — a line chart you scrub, a select that morphs into its list, a number field that pushes back at its limit. Installs through the shadcn CLI, and ships an MCP server so an agent can read the catalogue and build from it rather than being told what exists.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier of components. Pro is $199 once for lifetime access to everything, including the blocks.
notes: Closest fit to how we already work of anything in this batch: shadcn CLI, Next.js, components we own the source of once they are installed. The MCP server is the differentiator — the agent can see the library instead of guessing at class names.
Blocks are the part that saves real time: whole flows (scheduling, triage, onboarding) rather than single controls.
Every example on the site is live rather than a recording, which is the right way to publish a motion library and makes it quick to judge before paying.

entries.name: Tenor
entries.what: A canvas for refining React interfaces by conversation: bring in the UI a coding agent produced or a reference for what you meant, compare variants side by side, then carry on in Codex, Claude or Cursor, or export the React.
entries.priceDetail: Pro $22/month billed annually. A custom plan for studios bringing it into client work is priced by conversation — no figure published. Mac app listed as coming soon.
notes: The pitch that separates it from the rest of this crowded category is the handoff: it is meant to sit between the agent that wrote the first pass and the agent that finishes it, not to replace either.
No free tier published, so judging it means paying for a month first.
Included AI usage refreshes monthly with no number attached to it, which is the thing to pin down before putting it anywhere near a client deadline.

entries.name: Liquid Glass (Glass SDK)
entries.what: Apple's Liquid Glass material as React components for the web and Electron — the Clear and Regular variants, progressive blur, edge refraction — built on WebGPU with WGSL shaders rather than stacked CSS filters.
entries.priceDetail: MIT licensed, published as @glass-sdk/liquid-glass.
notes: Version 0.0.2, first published days ago. MIT and open, but that version number is the headline: do not put it on the critical path of anything with a deadline.
WebGPU and WGSL under the hood, so support is the question to answer before adopting — a fallback path matters more here than the material does.
Worth watching rather than reaching for. If Liquid Glass keeps spreading through client briefs, having a real implementation rather than a CSS pastiche will matter.

entries.name: Anatomy
entries.what: A Claude Code skill that answers 'how does this work' by building the machine that does it: name an idea in one line and it draws a live isometric figure of hundreds of small parts you can turn, press and read, where every number on screen comes from the same model that moves it. Installs with `npx skills add wheresryan`; also runs in OpenCode and Codex.
entries.priceDetail: MIT licensed, source at github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy.
notes: The argument behind it is the useful part: boxes and arrows tell you the parts exist but not what they do, and leave the reader to imagine the motion. Worth stealing for how we explain architecture in a proposal whether or not we run the skill.
Not fast. The worked example — a mechanical watch movement — took just under two hours of agent time in one pass, so this is a considered deliverable, not something to run mid-call.
Output is SVG, WebGL and 3D, so a figure drops into a page or a doc rather than needing a tool to view it.

entries.name: OpenRouter
entries.what: One API and one bill in front of 500+ models from most of the providers, with automatic routing and failover between them, prompt caching, bring-your-own-key, and routing you can pin to EU or US regions.
entries.priceDetail: Free tier: 25+ free models, 4 free providers, 50 requests a day, community support. Standard is pay-as-you-go on a 5.5% platform fee; Business 8% and adds SSO/SAML, admin controls, policy-based routing and contractual SLAs; Enterprise is by contract.
notes: The reason to care on client work is the boring one: a single vendor relationship and one invoice across providers, plus failover when a provider has a bad afternoon.

The platform fee is a real line in a margin — 5.5% or 8% on top of token cost — so for a project pinned to one model it is cheaper to go direct. It earns its keep where you are switching models or hedging.
In-region routing and a DPA above the free tier are what make it answerable to a client's procurement, which most aggregator layers cannot do.

entries.name: Sindre Sorhus — Apps
entries.takeaway: One developer's catalogue of 61 Mac, iOS, Watch and Vision apps built over eleven years, filtered by platform and by free, paid or Setapp. Most are single-purpose and tiny — menu bar spacing, a .DS_Store inspector, world clocks, copying text that will not select — and a good number are open source.
entries.whatToDo: Reference and a source of small fixes. Action: run the free menu-bar utilities past the team as a kit, and read the Tiny Apps section before anyone proposes building an internal tool that already exists here.
notes: Also the clearest working argument for the one-job app: 61 of them, 6M+ users, sustained by one person, with a stated 10,000 support emails answered. Worth showing to a client who wants everything in version one.

entries.name: 404s.design
entries.takeaway: A gallery of error pages worth landing on, tagged three ways: style (brutalist, editorial, hand-drawn, large type), interaction (animated, custom cursor, game, scroll-driven) and industry, so you can pull the ones from agencies or fintech specifically. Keyboard shortcuts for grid and a random pick; submissions open.
entries.whatToDo: Reference for the page everyone leaves to last. Action: pick two from the Game and Interactive tags next time a 404 is in scope, rather than shipping the default.
notes: The industry filter is what makes it more than a mood board — it is quick to find what a competitor in a client's sector did.

entries.name: Expo demos
entries.takeaway: Thirty worked demos of things built with Expo, each credited to the person who made it and tagged by technique — WebGPU model viewers and bird flocks, Skia shaders, iOS liquid-glass curved tab bars, dynamic island scroll-collapse, native paste inputs, SwiftUI interop, gesture work.
entries.whatToDo: Reference when scoping React Native work. Action: check this before quoting on a native-feeling interaction — several of the things clients assume need a native build are demonstrated here running in Expo.
notes: Useful as evidence as much as reference: it is a short answer to 'can React Native do that properly', with a named author to each one.

entries.name: Treatments.gallery
entries.takeaway: 4,884 App Store product page headers alongside years of Google Play feature graphics, searchable by app, developer, category or colour, on an endless canvas that wraps in every direction. Curated by The Screenshot First Company, a studio that does App Store screenshots for a living.
