entries.whatToDo: Reference for app store creative, which usually gets designed last and worst. Action: search the client's category before drawing a store header, and use the Play feature graphics as the head start they are — Play has run that format for years, Apple's header is new.
notes: Colour search is the genuinely useful filter: it finds the headers that will sit next to a client's brand rather than ones that merely look good alone.

entries.name: Spotted in Prod
entries.takeaway: Standout iOS interactions, captured as clips and tagged more finely than anything comparable: by style, by the gesture that triggers it (scrub, pull, flick, gyroscope, long press), by the screen it lives on (paywall, empty state, permissions, onboarding), by the pattern (bottom sheet, shared element, card stack) and by the size of company that shipped it. Carries a jobs board too.
entries.whatToDo: Reference with a real search behind it. Action: when a client asks for a specific feel, search the gesture or the screen type rather than scrolling a feed, and take the clip into the kickoff as the shared reference.
notes: The 'Startup / Indie / Big Co / Small Co' filter is quietly the most useful one — it keeps you from pitching an interaction that took a platform team a quarter.

entries.name: Victor Murea
entries.takeaway: A freelance brand designer's site, built around a small number of case studies rather than a wall of work — a divorce law firm and a YC-backed data engineering tool among them — with client testimonials carrying most of the persuading.
entries.whatToDo: Reference for how a solo brand practice presents itself. Action: compare the case-study-plus-testimonial structure against how our own work pages are built before the next site refresh.
notes: Filed as portfolio inspiration. If it was sent as a possible collaborator or hire rather than as reference, it belongs in the CRM and not on this site — say so and I will pull it.

entries.name: CTA.gallery
entries.takeaway: A gallery of calls to action pulled off real sites, sorted by what the thing actually is — button, newsletter, pricing block, download, modal, navigation, call-to-buy — and filterable by industry and by light or dark. Carries CTA writing tips alongside the visuals.
entries.whatToDo: Reference for the component that decides whether a page works. Action: pull the pricing and newsletter sets before designing a conversion block, and filter by the client's industry rather than browsing the lot.
notes: Sorting by CTA type rather than by site is what makes it quicker than a general gallery — you are looking for one component, not a whole page.
Heavily sponsored with template ads mixed into the grid, so the listings and the adverts need reading apart.

entries.name: Footer.design
entries.takeaway: Sixty-five pages of website footers, tagged by type and style — typographic, illustrative, grid, animated, cards, large type, bright, dark — with an editor's pick running through it.
entries.whatToDo: Reference for the section that always gets designed last and least. Action: agree a footer direction from here at the same time as the hero, instead of improvising one the week before launch.
notes: Narrow by design and better for it: one page section, properly tagged, rather than a thousand homepages you have to scroll past the fold of.

entries.name: Supahero
entries.takeaway: A hand-picked library of website hero sections — several hundred, mostly agency, SaaS and portfolio work — presented as a plain searchable grid.
entries.whatToDo: Reference for the first screen. Action: use it to put three hero directions in front of a client at kickoff rather than describing them.
notes: The site now announces that Supahero is part of Screensdesign, an app-UX library. Still live and still free at this URL, but treat it as a collection under new ownership rather than an actively growing product, and check it is still there before relying on it.

entries.name: Dark
entries.takeaway: Hand-picked dark-themed websites, sorted by sector — agency, AI, culture, education, hardware, personal, software, web3 — and by new or popular. A separate templates section sits alongside the gallery.
entries.whatToDo: Reference for when a brief lands on dark. Action: filter to the client's sector before the first concept, since dark done for a hardware brand and dark done for an agency are not the same decision.
notes: Browsing is free; accounts exist for monthly picks. Run by Y5K LLC.
A narrow gallery that earns the narrowness — dark layouts fail in specific ways, and seeing a few dozen that work is more useful than a general feed.

entries.name: Coolest
entries.takeaway: Weekly hand-picked design work across websites, brand identity, motion and product, each with a written note explaining what the piece is and what is interesting about it rather than just a thumbnail.
entries.whatToDo: Reference and a weekly read. Action: put it in the team channel as a Friday link — the written notes make it discussable, which a wall of screenshots is not.
notes: The short write-up under each entry is the differentiator. Most galleries show you the picture and leave you to work out why it was chosen.

entries.name: Yee
entries.what: A link-in-bio that grows into an actual website: start from a template, then add a shop for digital products, bookings against your availability, contact forms, a blog and as many pages as you need, with submissions landing in one dashboard.
entries.priceDetail: Free forever: 1 live site, unlimited drafts, all themes, 50MB media, Yee branding. Pro $6/month or $49/year (a 32% saving): 3 live sites, own domain on each, shop, bookings, custom code, no branding, 1GB media. Checkout via Polar, prices exclude VAT.
notes: Not for client work — it is a hosted builder on someone else's domain model, and we build sites. Where it could earn its place is a one-page holding site or a personal page for someone in the team, done in an hour rather than a day.
The bookings and shop sections are the only parts that would be real work to replicate; the rest is a page builder.
50MB of media on the free tier is the limit that will bite first.

entries.name: Backgrounds Supply
entries.what: A library of backgrounds, wallpapers and gradients — part handcrafted, part AI-generated — for presentations, social, banners, websites and apps, with a gradient tool alongside it.
entries.priceDetail: A freebies section, then $49 one-time for unlimited access to the full library. That is the figure the site serves; it publishes no tiers.
notes: Useful for the job it names: the deck or landing page that needs a backdrop today and does not warrant commissioning one.
Part of the library is AI-generated and the site does not spell out the licence on the way in. Worth reading the terms before anything goes on a client's homepage rather than a pitch deck.
The marketing is loud — 'are you facing these issues' — which says more about who it is sold to than what it is. The assets are the thing; ignore the page.

entries.name: Screen Movie
entries.what: A native macOS screen recorder with a real editor behind it: multiple timeline tracks and scenes, animated text, images and captions, device mockups, motion backgrounds, music and 4K export — aimed at product videos rather than bug reports.
entries.priceDetail: $39 one-time. Version 1.3, updated 5 October 2026. Requires macOS 15 or later.
notes: Fills the gap between a raw recording and an editing suite — the thing you actually need for a client demo, a release note or a case-study video.
One-time purchase and native, so no subscription and no Electron, which is the difference between using it and dreading it.
macOS 15+ and a small maker — stated as used by 150+ people — so it is a one-developer dependency. Fine for internal use, worth knowing before it becomes part of a delivery process.

entries.name: Icoon
entries.what: A library of 1,500+ AI-generated 3D icons, illustrations, characters, mockups and shapes in SVG, PNG and editable PSD, with a mockup generator alongside it.
entries.priceDetail: Freebies section, then $29 one-time (listed down from $59) for lifetime access to everything, stated as covering personal and client work under a commercial licence. Monthly options also offered.
notes: The commercial licence covering client work is stated plainly on the pricing page, which is more than most asset libraries manage — but it is the vendor's own assertion, so read the licence page before it goes in a deliverable.
Every asset is AI-generated. That is fine for a deck or an internal tool and a conversation with some clients' legal teams, so ask before it reaches a brand page.
Editable PSD alongside SVG and PNG is the useful part: a 3D icon you cannot recolour to a brand palette is a 3D icon you use once.

entries.name: Insposite
entries.takeaway: Five pages of links in three buckets — developer portfolios, inspiration galleries and web tools — each credited to the handle behind it. A one-person index by Prasanjit Dey, meant as a replacement for a bookmarks folder.
entries.whatToDo: Reference, thinly. Action: skim the Portfolio bucket, which is the part we do not already cover, and ignore the rest.
notes: It is a directory of directories: the Inspiration bucket lists Awwwards, Siteinspire and SEESAW, and the Tools bucket lists things we already carry. For us that makes most of it a layer we do not need, since this toolbox is the curated list.
The footer reads 2025 and the index is short, so treat it as a snapshot rather than something being kept current.
The developer portfolios are the one genuinely distinct part, and the only reason it is here rather than skipped.

entries.name: Modulify
entries.what: An AI site and app builder aimed at shipping rather than prototyping: describe what you want, get a working site or internal tool with a database, auth, realtime and analytics behind it, and a library of production templates you clone into your dashboard rather than download.
entries.priceDetail: Free: 35 one-off AI credits, 1 site, Modulify subdomain and branding. Starter $20/month billed yearly (20% saving) for 100 credits a month, custom domain and branding removed. Higher tiers and enterprise above that.
notes: Credits rather than seats is the pricing model to watch — 100 a month is the number to sanity-check against a real project before committing.
The templates page is free to browse and clone, which is the cheapest way to judge the output quality before paying.

Worth knowing it sits at the centre of a cluster of design-resource sites that all link to it, including an 'independent' ranking that puts it first. That is marketing, not a verdict on the product — judge it on the build.

entries.name: Wedoflow
entries.what: 216 premium Webflow templates covering 1,300+ pages — agency, SaaS, portfolio, medical, finance, education — sold individually or as an all-access pass, with cloneable components alongside.
entries.priceDetail: Individual templates $79–$169. An all-access pass to the whole library plus monthly releases is sold at a heavily and permanently discounted headline — the site was showing 95% off across everything, which is the real price rather than a sale.
notes: Only relevant where a client is already on Webflow. For anything we build in Next.js it is reference at best.
The permanent-countdown, permanent-95%-off presentation is a flag on how the business is run, not on the templates, which look competent. Judge the files, ignore the banner.

Part of a cluster: every one of the sixteen sites sent over in this batch links out to Modulify, and this one, Landdding, LogoToUse, FontInLogo, Wonderlist and Wedoflow cross-link each other. Useful on its own terms; just do not read the cross-promotion as independent endorsement.

entries.name: Wonderlist
entries.what: 127 website designs delivered as Figma files rather than code — 1,137 pages across SaaS, agency, portfolio, finance, real estate and more, with a font pack and stated MIT-licensed images and fonts.
entries.priceDetail: Lite $329 for 25 designs and 212 pages, single-user licence, unlimited projects. Higher bundles at $599 and $999. Sold as buy-once with live updates, discounted on a running promotion.
notes: Figma rather than code is the point: these are a starting layout for a designer, not something to hand a developer.

It states that bundled images and fonts are MIT licensed and usable on unlimited projects under a single-user licence. Read the licence against how many of us would open the file before buying — single-user is the constraint that bites in a studio.

Part of a cluster: every one of the sixteen sites sent over in this batch links out to Modulify, and this one, Landdding, LogoToUse, FontInLogo, Wonderlist and Wedoflow cross-link each other. Useful on its own terms; just do not read the cross-promotion as independent endorsement.

entries.name: Motion (motionin.design)
entries.what: Physics-based, cursor-responsive web sections — scatter walls, immersive heroes, product showcases — sold not as code but as prompts: you copy a long, very specific written spec and paste it into an AI model to generate the section.
entries.priceDetail: A free tier of sections alongside paid ones. Individual prices run from the mid-twenties up, with a bundle at $149.
notes: The format is the interesting bit and the risk at once. What you buy is a prompt, so the output depends on your model and your luck, and two runs will not match. Read one of the free specs before paying for any of them.
The specs themselves are a lesson in writing motion briefs — they describe easing, bleed, loop and feel in a level of detail most of us never put in writing.

Part of a cluster: every one of the sixteen sites sent over in this batch links out to Modulify, and this one, Landdding, LogoToUse, FontInLogo, Wonderlist and Wedoflow cross-link each other. Useful on its own terms; just do not read the cross-promotion as independent endorsement.

entries.name: LogoToUse
entries.what: A library of other companies' brand marks — colour, solid black and knockout white versions of several hundred recognisable logos — as SVG, PNG and editable Figma, for mockups, decks and template placeholders.
entries.priceDetail: Free to browse with no account. Pro from $5/month adds SVG, Figma and bulk ZIP downloads.
notes: Name the obvious risk: these are third-party trademarks, and no library can license you someone else's mark. The 'commercial licence on Pro' covers their service, not Nike's or PayPal's rights. Fine in an internal mockup; a conversation with legal the moment it appears in a client's 'trusted by' row or anything published.
What it is genuinely good for is the dummy logo wall in a pitch deck or template, where you need recognisable shapes at the right weight and would otherwise spend an hour on it.

Part of a cluster: every one of the sixteen sites sent over in this batch links out to Modulify, and this one, Landdding, LogoToUse, FontInLogo, Wonderlist and Wedoflow cross-link each other. Useful on its own terms; just do not read the cross-promotion as independent endorsement.

entries.name: Ikonik
entries.what: 50,000+ open-source icons gathered from 45-odd icon projects into one browser, with a built-in editor for size, stroke and colour, and copy-as-HTML or download-as-SVG on the spot.
entries.priceDetail: Free. The icons are the upstream projects' own, under whatever licence each carries.
notes: A search box across 45 icon sets is the useful thing here — it saves the usual round of opening four sites to find one glyph.
Because it aggregates other people's sets, the licence that matters is the source project's, not this site's. Check which pack an icon came from before it ships.

Part of a cluster: every one of the sixteen sites sent over in this batch links out to Modulify, and this one, Landdding, LogoToUse, FontInLogo, Wonderlist and Wedoflow cross-link each other. Useful on its own terms; just do not read the cross-promotion as independent endorsement.

entries.name: Modulify Logo Maker
entries.what: Describe a business in one sentence and get a finished logo plus the print-ready files — PNG, SVG, PDF and EPS — with a public gallery of everything made with it.
entries.priceDetail: One free logo a day. $19 once to take a mark away with the vector files.
notes: Nothing here replaces identity work and it does not pretend to — it is aimed at founders and side projects without a budget.

Where it could earn a place with us is the throwaway mark: a placeholder for a prototype, a fake brand in a pitch deck, a logo for an internal tool. $19 and thirty seconds beats an hour of someone's time.
Generated marks carry no originality guarantee and the gallery is public by default, so nothing client-confidential should go near the brief box.

Part of a cluster: every one of the sixteen sites sent over in this batch links out to Modulify, and this one, Landdding, LogoToUse, FontInLogo, Wonderlist and Wedoflow cross-link each other. Useful on its own terms; just do not read the cross-promotion as independent endorsement.

entries.name: closeit.fast
entries.what: Electronic signatures without the enterprise tax: drop in a PDF, place signature, initial and date fields, send a secure link, and get back a sealed, tamper-evident document with an audit trail.
entries.priceDetail: Free to start. One plan at $12 per user per month, or $72 a year per user (an effective $6/month). Every feature in both, unlimited envelopes and recipients, nothing per signature.
notes: The pricing is the pitch: per-signature charging is what makes the incumbents expensive for a studio sending a handful of SOWs a month.
Before it touches a real contract, check what its audit trail and seal actually amount to against eIDAS or whatever the client's counsel expects. 'Tamper-evident' is a claim, not a standard.
Unknown operator and no stated company behind it, which for the system holding signed client contracts is the question to answer first.

Part of a cluster: every one of the sixteen sites sent over in this batch links out to Modulify, and this one, Landdding, LogoToUse, FontInLogo, Wonderlist and Wedoflow cross-link each other. Useful on its own terms; just do not read the cross-promotion as independent endorsement.

entries.name: Sent
entries.what: One API across SMS, WhatsApp and RCS that handles routing, formatting, compliance and delivery itself, with SDKs for Node, Python, Go and Ruby.
entries.priceDetail: Per message, by channel and destination — the published rates run from about $0.0047 to $0.053 a message. No platform fee or seat cost published; enterprise by conversation.
notes: RCS alongside SMS and WhatsApp is the reason to look: verified branded messaging is what clients ask for once they have seen it, and wiring it up directly is weeks of work.
Compliance handled upstream matters more than it sounds — the sender registration regimes are the part that delays launches, not the sending.
Independent of the Modulify cluster the rest of this batch belongs to; it appears there only as a customer logo.

entries.name: Paper Animation
entries.what: Turns an uploaded image into short paper-craft animations — folded paper, animated newspaper clippings with justified columns and period typefaces, magazine cut-out lettering, fake press coverage — aimed at social clips.
entries.priceDetail: Free to try in the browser with no card. Paid tiers from the low tens of dollars.
notes: Squarely a creator tool for TikTok and Reels, not a studio tool. Listed because the newspaper-clipping effect is a recognisable brief that occasionally lands, and this does it in seconds.
The fake-press-coverage output is the part to be careful with: a fabricated newspaper page about a real client is a reputational problem waiting to happen, however obviously stylised.

Part of a cluster: every one of the sixteen sites sent over in this batch links out to Modulify, and this one, Landdding, LogoToUse, FontInLogo, Wonderlist and Wedoflow cross-link each other. Useful on its own terms; just do not read the cross-promotion as independent endorsement.

entries.name: DomainGrowth
entries.what: A paid backlink service: it sells contextual, permanent link placements on ten design and no-code websites the operator says they own and maintain, with domain ratings up to 70, sold in capped monthly batches.
entries.priceDetail: Sold as credit packages, with published figures running from around $110 up to $599. A free account exists to view the network.
notes: This is a private blog network. Paying for links that pass ranking signal is against Google's link spam policy, and the consequence lands on the client's domain, not on the vendor's. Do not put this near client SEO work.
It is listed rather than skipped so there is a written answer when someone forwards it. The answer is no.

It also explains the rest of this batch: the ten sites it sells placements on match the design and no-code resource sites sent over alongside it, which is why they all cross-link. Read those cross-links as inventory, not endorsement.

entries.name: Landdding
entries.takeaway: A daily-updated gallery of landing pages and website designs with community upvoting, sliced by a long list of industries from SaaS and fintech to charity, gaming and weather.
entries.whatToDo: Reference. Action: filter to the client's industry at concept stage; the industry list is finer-grained than most galleries manage.
notes: Upvotes make it closer to a feed than a curation, so the top of it reflects what designers liked that week rather than what works.

Part of a cluster: every one of the sixteen sites sent over in this batch links out to Modulify, and this one, Landdding, LogoToUse, FontInLogo, Wonderlist and Wedoflow cross-link each other. Useful on its own terms; just do not read the cross-promotion as independent endorsement.

entries.name: Iconly
entries.takeaway: An inspiration library of 2,400+ app, game and web app icons from real products — Spotify, Monzo, Strava, Revolut, Headspace — searchable by category, style and colour. Reference only, not a download library.
entries.whatToDo: Reference for app icon work, which is usually designed in a vacuum. Action: pull the set from the client's category before sketching, and use the colour filter to see what the shelf actually looks like.
notes: That it shows real shipped icons rather than dribbble concepts is the whole value: an app icon is judged next to its competitors at 60 pixels, and this is the only way to see that.

Part of a cluster: every one of the sixteen sites sent over in this batch links out to Modulify, and this one, Landdding, LogoToUse, FontInLogo, Wonderlist and Wedoflow cross-link each other. Useful on its own terms; just do not read the cross-promotion as independent endorsement.

entries.name: Font In Logo
entries.takeaway: Identifies the typefaces behind well-known brand, film and game logos, with a verified section for source-checked matches, grouped by industry and by typeface, plus a generator for previewing your own text in any of them.
entries.whatToDo: Reference for type direction conversations. Action: when a client says 'something like that logo', look it up here and put the actual typeface on the table instead of guessing.
notes: The verified-versus-unverified split is what makes it usable; most 'what font is that' sites do not distinguish a confirmed match from a guess.
Identifying a typeface is not licensing it — the font behind a famous logo is often custom or heavily modified, and the one named here may be the base rather than the final.

Part of a cluster: every one of the sixteen sites sent over in this batch links out to Modulify, and this one, Landdding, LogoToUse, FontInLogo, Wonderlist and Wedoflow cross-link each other. Useful on its own terms; just do not read the cross-promotion as independent endorsement.

entries.name: BestAIBuilder
entries.takeaway: An index of 101 AI website builders, each given the same brief and scored out of 100 on craft, speed, control and value, with 18 fully reviewed at the time of reading.
entries.whatToDo: Read the methodology, not the ranking. Action: use its identical-brief approach as a template for our own comparison when a client asks which AI builder to standardise on.
notes: It states 'no sponsored slots and no affiliate ordering' and then ranks Modulify first of 101, ahead of Lovable and v0 — and it links to Modulify, as does every other site in the batch it arrived with. Treat the ordering as marketing for the thing at the top.
The method underneath is sound and worth borrowing: one identical brief, four named criteria, published scores. It is the independence claim that does not survive checking.
Index last refreshed July 2026 against a field that moves monthly.

entries.name: Whipsaw — Work
entries.takeaway: The full project archive of Whipsaw, a long-running industrial design consultancy — 176 projects filterable by service (brand, digital, physical) and by industry from robotics and biotech to mobility and healthcare, each a real shipped product rather than a concept.
entries.whatToDo: Reference for how a mature consultancy presents hardware-plus-digital work. Action: read three case studies before writing the next proposal that spans physical and digital, and note how they scope the brand layer alongside both.
notes: The service filter is the useful part for us: seeing the same studio's brand, digital and physical work on one project is rare and is close to how our own cross-discipline jobs run.
Independent of the rest of this batch — a genuine consultancy portfolio, not part of the link network.

entries.name: Mebius Free Charts
entries.what: 62 free chart cards for dashboards and analytics, shipped twice over: a Figma file and animated React with TypeScript and Tailwind v4, installable through the shadcn CLI. By Keitoto Studio, whose paid UI kits sit alongside.
entries.priceDetail: The 62 charts are free. The wider dashboard, mobile and website UI kits are pay-once with every update included, sold through Polar.
notes: Design and code of the same component from one source is the rare part — most chart libraries give you one or the other and leave someone to reconcile them.
shadcn CLI and Tailwind v4 means it drops straight into how we already build, with the source in our repo rather than a dependency.
Free preview before paying is stated plainly, so the kits can be judged on the charts.
Independent of the rest of this batch.

entries.name: Superhuman Prompt Library
entries.takeaway: 123 prompt packs across 14 disciplines, 1,076 prompts in total, free and with no sign-up or paywall. Every prompt is a fillable template — a role line, bracketed context fields, numbered instructions, a fixed output format, a missing-information policy and a quality bar. Run by the Superhuman newsletter (Zain Kahn).
entries.whatToDo: Read the Engineering packs; use our own prompts for everything else. Action: compare a Superhuman pack against the Gitwork prompt on the same topic in the starter library before deciding which to paste.
notes: The quality is two-tier, and it is measurable. Scoring every numbered instruction in all 123 packs for whether it names a concrete failure mode, Engineering comes out at 46% at an average of 148 characters a step. The next best of the other thirteen disciplines is Legal at 17%, and most sit between 5% and 15% at around 60 characters — 'avoid biased wording', 'keep language neutral'. Engineering is a quarter of the library by volume and almost all of its value.
No relation to Superhuman the email client (superhuman.com), which is already on this list. Different company, different product, same word — this one is Zain Kahn's newsletter at superhuman.ai.

Several non-engineering prompts are topic-locked rather than templated — the market-research one is written for the beauty industry, the SEO one for adventure travel — so you are rewriting the domain before you can use them anyway.

Copyright Superhuman Newsletter, no licence published — these are linked, not copied. Lifting the text into the Foundry starter library would be republishing someone else's work, so treat them as reference and write our own version of anything we want to keep.

Written for ChatGPT and shaped for it: a role line, bracketed fields, a fixed output format and a missing-information policy. They transfer to Claude unchanged but carry no tool use, no file context and no agent loop, so they are a starting draft rather than a skill.

The 107 packs outside Engineering are not listed individually here. Their topics were rewritten as 82 Gitwork prompts in the starter library instead — ours, so they can be edited and used on client work, and measurably stronger: 58% of their instructions name a concrete failure mode against 46% for this site's best category and 19% across it as a whole.

entries.name: Web Development prompts (Superhuman)
entries.takeaway: 25 fillable ChatGPT prompts for web development, including “Build a Responsive Navigation System with Grid, Flexbox, and Mobile Menu States”, “Write a Reusable JavaScript Form Validation Module”, “Design a Theme Preference System with Persistence, Accessibility, and Rendering Safety”. Measured over the whole pack, 40% of the numbered instructions in a prompt name a concrete failure mode rather than a generic rule, at an average of 142 characters a step.
entries.whatToDo: Reference, and the best pack on the site. Action: read the navigation, Tailwind-adoption and WordPress-to-React prompts before the next front-end rebuild and lift the failure-mode lists into our own brief.
notes: The failure modes are the value, not the prompts: a mobile menu with no focus trap, sticky-header stacking-context conflicts, breakpoint logic duplicated between media queries and JS resize listeners, a hamburger missing aria-expanded. That is a review checklist we can use whether or not anyone runs the prompt.

Copyright Superhuman Newsletter, no licence published — these are linked, not copied. Lifting the text into the Foundry starter library would be republishing someone else's work, so treat them as reference and write our own version of anything we want to keep.

entries.name: Software Development prompts (Superhuman)
entries.takeaway: 20 fillable ChatGPT prompts for software development, including “Write Python Registration Validation with Structured Errors and Password Policy Checks”, “Design and Implement a Flask REST API with Resource Boundaries, Validation, and Production-Ready Basics”, “Design a Unit Test Strategy for a JavaScript Pricing Function with Edge-Case and Change-Risk Coverage”. Measured over the whole pack, 46% of the numbered instructions in a prompt name a concrete failure mode rather than a generic rule, at an average of 162 characters a step.
entries.whatToDo: Reference. Action: compare its version-control and unit-test-strategy prompts against our own Launch Kit rules and close any gap.
notes: Covers the unglamorous half — ESLint and Prettier with pre-commit hooks, Docker for a Node and Mongo dev environment, structured validation errors — which is where client handovers usually fail.

entries.promptText:
You are a market researcher who has seen research decks get commissioned, read once and change nothing. Your job is to design research that forces a decision, not to produce a survey.

Design the market research below.

Context:
- The decision this research has to inform: [decision]
- Who we are and what we sell: [company]
- Audience or segment: [audience]
- Market or geography: [market]
- What we already believe, and how confident we are: [priors]
- Budget, timeline and access constraints: [constraints]

Instructions:
1. Start from the decision, not the questions. If the stated decision would be the same whatever the research returns, say so and stop — research commissioned to ratify a decision already made is the most common way a research budget fails to change anything.
2. Name the specific belief each question is trying to break, and cut any question that can only confirm what we already think — that is the confirmation bias risk, and it is what produces a deck everyone agrees with and nobody acts on.
3. Choose the method against the decision's reversibility and the budget: desk research and five customer calls beat a 300-response survey for anything qualitative, and a survey under about 100 responses per segment cannot support the cross-tabs people will inevitably ask for.
4. Ask about past behaviour rather than future intent. Stated purchase intent is an unreliable predictor of real conversion, and ranking questions with more than about seven options collect noise rather than preference — avoid both.
5. Flag where the sample will be biased before it is collected — recruiting from our own list, our own social channels or an incentivised panel each skew in a known direction, and that skew has to be written next to the finding, not discovered afterwards.
6. Define in advance what result would change the decision, and what would not. Write the thresholds down before fielding.

Output format:
- The decision, restated in one line
- Beliefs under test, with current confidence
- Recommended method and why, with the rejected alternatives
- Question set or discussion guide
- Sampling plan and its known biases
- Decision thresholds agreed before fielding
- Cost, timeline and what we will not learn

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if the decision or the audience is unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Produce a generic questionnaire that could be sent to any market.
- Use leading or double-barrelled questions, or a five-point scale where a behavioural question would do.
- Promise statistical significance that the proposed sample size cannot deliver.

Quality bar:
- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are a product marketing manager who has watched launches fail because the positioning was agreed in a document nobody outside marketing ever read.

Build the product marketing work below.

Context:
- Product and what it actually does: [product]
- Who it is for, and who it is not for: [audience]
- The alternative they use today, including doing nothing: [alternative]
- Proof we can stand behind: [proof]
- Launch date and channels: [launch]
- Internal teams who must repeat this: [teams]

Instructions:
1. Write the positioning against the real alternative, which is usually a spreadsheet, an agency or doing nothing — positioning against the competitor the sales team likes to name is the most common way a launch fails to land with people who have never heard of that competitor.
2. Separate claims we can evidence from claims we would like to be true, and mark each one. An unevidenced claim repeated by a salesperson in a deal is a commercial risk, not a messaging choice.
3. Test the one-line description against the 'so what' question three times. If it survives only because the reader already knows the product, it has failed — avoid describing the category where a buyer would expect an outcome.
4. Name what the product does badly or does not do, and where that should be said out loud. Launches that hide a known gap generate support load and churn in the first ninety days instead of objections in the first week.
5. Write the enablement in the words the sales and support teams will actually use, not the words in the deck. Positioning that only exists in a PDF does not survive contact with a customer call.
6. Define the launch's success measure before the date, and distinguish activity metrics (posts, views) from the one that matters (qualified pipeline, activation, retention).

Output format:
- Positioning statement and the alternative it is written against
- Claim table: claim, evidence, owner, risk if challenged
- One-liner, short description and long description
- Known gaps and the line we take on each
- Enablement notes for sales and support
- Launch plan with success measure and the metrics we are deliberately ignoring

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if the real alternative or the audience is unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Write positioning that would fit any product in the category.
- Claim a benefit without naming the evidence behind it.
- Describe the product in terms of its features where a buyer would ask about an outcome.

Quality bar:
- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are a creative strategist who briefs work that has to perform, not work that has to win an award.

Build the creative strategy below.

Context:
- Brand and what it sells: [brand]
- Audience and what they currently believe: [audience]
- The behaviour we want to change: [behaviour]
- Channels and formats: [channels]
- What has already been tried, and what happened: [history]
- Budget and production constraints: [constraints]

Instructions:
1. Name the single belief the work has to shift. A strategy that lists three audiences and four messages is a scheduling document rather than a strategy, and it fails at the first budget cut because nothing in it is load-bearing.
2. Write the insight as something a real person would recognise about themselves, uncomfortable included. An insight nobody would admit to out loud is usually the true one; an insight that flatters the audience is usually a category truism.
3. Separate the idea from the executions. An idea that only works in one format is an execution, and the risk is discovering that halfway through production when the channel plan changes.
4. Design for the first two seconds in feed and the first five on video. Work that needs a setup before it makes sense is routinely cut off by the platform before the setup lands.
5. Name the executions most likely to fail review — legal, brand safety, accessibility of on-screen text, contrast of captions — before production rather than at the sign-off meeting.
6. Define what would make us kill the idea, and when we check. Creative with no kill criterion runs until the budget is spent, which is a slow and avoidable failure.

Output format:
- The belief to shift, in one line
- Insight and why it is uncomfortable
- The idea, stated so it survives any channel
- Three executions, with the format constraints each respects
- Risks at review, and the pre-emptive answer to each
- Kill criteria and the point at which we check them

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if the behaviour to change or the channel is unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Offer an idea that is really a tagline.
- Write an insight that the audience would find flattering and unobjectionable.
- Propose executions without saying how they open in the first two seconds.

Quality bar:
- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are an email marketer who is judged on revenue per send and list health, not on open rate.

Design the email programme below.

Context:
- Offer and audience: [offer]
- List source, size and age: [list]
- Sending platform and current deliverability: [platform]
- Cadence we can actually sustain: [cadence]
- What we have sent before and how it performed: [history]
- Commercial goal: [goal]

Instructions:
1. Optimise for reply, click and revenue per recipient, not open rate — Apple Mail Privacy Protection pre-fetches images, so an open-rate-driven programme is tuned against a metric that has been unreliable since 2021.
2. Check list health before creative. Sending to an old or bought list risks spam-trap hits and a domain reputation that takes months to repair, and no subject line survives landing in spam.
3. Segment by behaviour rather than by demographic, and say what each segment is allowed to receive — the failure mode is one audience getting three unrelated campaigns in a week and unsubscribing from all of them.

5. Set the unsubscribe and preference path to be obvious. Hiding it increases spam complaints, which damages the sending domain far more than the lost subscriber does.
6. Define the holdout. Without a group that receives nothing, attributed revenue cannot be distinguished from revenue that would have arrived anyway.

Output format:
- Programme map: segment, trigger, message, frequency cap
- Deliverability checks to clear before the first send
- Email-by-email outline with plain-text first
- Measurement plan with holdout and the metrics we ignore
- List-health actions and the suppression rules
- Assumptions and risks

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if list source or the commercial goal is unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Report open rate as a primary success measure.
- Propose a cadence the team cannot sustain past week three.
- Write subject lines that misrepresent the contents of the email.

- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are a paid social buyer who has to defend the spend, across Meta, TikTok, YouTube and X, and who knows each platform's reporting flatters itself.

Plan the paid social activity below.

Context:

- Audience and the platform(s) in scope: [audience]

- Creative we already have: [assets]

Instructions:
1. Fix measurement before spend. Platform-reported conversions use view-through and modelled attribution and will not reconcile with the CRM — agree in advance which number is the one we are judged on, or the post-campaign meeting becomes an argument about whose dashboard is wrong.
2. Size the audience against the budget. An audience too small for the budget drives frequency up and performance down within days, and over-narrow targeting is a more common failure than over-broad.

- Measurement agreement: the number we are judged on, and why
- Audience and budget sizing with frequency ceiling
- Creative matrix: concept, format, hook, variant count
- Policy risks and pre-emptive fixes
- Kill and scale rules with thresholds

- What we stop doing

entries.promptText:
You are organising content for people who arrive from search and have never seen the navigation.

Design the information architecture below.

Context:
- Site or product and its content: [scope]
- Audiences and their tasks: [audiences]
- Current structure and its known problems: [current]
- Search and analytics data: [data]
- Who owns the content, and who adds to it: [owners]
- Migration or platform constraints: [constraints]

Instructions:
1. Structure by the user's task, not by the company's org chart. Navigation that mirrors internal departments is the standard failure of a corporate site, and it is invisible to the people who built it.
2. Assume most people land deep rather than on the homepage. A structure that only works from the top fails for search traffic, which is usually the majority.
3. Name things as users name them, using search query data where it exists. Internal jargon in a label is a silent failure — nobody complains, they just do not click.
4. Keep the primary navigation short enough to scan. Beyond roughly seven items people stop reading and start hunting, and adding one more item is how a menu degrades over years.
5. Design the growth path: where does the next section go, and who decides. An architecture with no rule for additions drifts back to a dumping ground within a year.
6. Plan URL changes and redirects alongside the structure, because an IA change without a redirect map discards accumulated search equity and the traffic loss is usually blamed on the design.

Output format:
- Task-based structure with the rationale
- Labels, with search evidence where available
- Primary navigation, kept scannable
- Deep-entry check: does each page stand alone
- Growth rule and owner
- URL and redirect plan

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if the audiences' tasks or the platform is unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Mirror the organisation chart.
- Use internal jargon as a label.
- Change URLs without a redirect plan.

Quality bar:
- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are producing a roadmap that someone will hold you to, so it has to be honest about uncertainty.

Prioritise the work below and build the roadmap.

Context:
- Candidate items: [items]
- The outcome we are optimising for: [outcome]
- Team capacity, including maintenance and support: [capacity]
- Dependencies and fixed dates: [dependencies]
- Confidence in each estimate: [confidence]
- Who must agree: [stakeholders]

Instructions:
1. Score against one outcome. Multi-criteria scoring frameworks mostly launder a decision already made, and the risk is a number that looks objective and is not.
2. Reserve capacity for maintenance, support and the unplanned before allocating any of it. A roadmap built on full capacity fails in the first month and takes the team's credibility with it.
3. Separate items by confidence and treat them differently — a well-understood item can be dated, where a genuinely uncertain one should carry a spike with a decision point, not a date.
4. Make dependencies explicit and name who owns each. An undeclared cross-team dependency is the most common reason a dated roadmap slips, and the risk is that it is discovered late enough to be unfixable.
5. Express the roadmap in horizons rather than dates where confidence is low, because a false date is more damaging to trust than an admitted range.
6. Write what gets dropped if something slips and agree it now rather than in the week it happens, to avoid the failure where everything stays on the plan and the quality goes instead.

Output format:
- Single outcome and the scoring against it
- Capacity after maintenance and support
- Items split by confidence, with spikes where needed
- Dependency map with owners
- Roadmap in horizons or dates, as confidence allows
- The drop list, agreed in advance

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if capacity or the outcome is unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Use a scoring framework to justify a decision already made.
- Allocate 100% of capacity.
- Give a date for work nobody understands yet.

Quality bar:
- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are writing the words inside a product, where a wrong word costs a support ticket.

Write the interface copy below.

Context:
- Screen, component or flow: [surface]
- What the user is trying to do: [job]
- What the system knows at this point: [state]
- Constraints: character limits, localisation, tone: [constraints]
- Error or edge cases in scope: [errors]
- Existing patterns we must match: [patterns]

Instructions:
1. Write the action, not the concept. A button labelled with a noun makes the user guess what happens, and guessing at a destructive action is how data gets deleted.
2. Write errors that say what happened, why, and what to do next. 'Something went wrong' is the standard failure of product copy and converts directly into support load.
3. Never blame the user. Copy that implies fault increases abandonment at exactly the moment the person is already stuck.
4. Check every string against its character limit in the narrowest supported language — copy that fits in English and breaks the layout in German is a defect found late and fixed expensively.
5. Be specific about irreversibility. A confirmation dialogue that does not say the action cannot be undone is the kind of omission that produces a complaint rather than a ticket.
6. Match the existing patterns or change them deliberately everywhere, because a product with three different words for the same object teaches users that the words do not matter.

Output format:
- Copy per state: default, empty, loading, success, error
- Button labels as actions
- Error messages with cause and next step
- Character counts against the limits
- Irreversible actions and their wording
- Terminology check against existing patterns

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if the system state or the character limits are unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Write an error that does not say what to do next.
- Label a destructive button with a noun.
- Imply the user is at fault.

Quality bar:
- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are running research with people who will try to be helpful, which is the main threat to the findings.

Plan and run the research below.

Context:
- The decision this informs: [decision]
- Who we need to speak to, and how we will reach them: [participants]
- What we currently believe: [assumptions]
- Method constraints: time, budget, remote or in person: [constraints]
- Product or prototype available: [artefact]
- Who will act on the findings: [audience]

Instructions:
1. Write the question the research must answer and check it is not already answered. Research run to build confidence rather than to learn something is a common and expensive failure.
2. Ask about past behaviour rather than hypothetical preference. People predict their own future behaviour badly, and a session full of 'would you use this' produces agreeable, unreliable answers.
3. Avoid leading the participant. A demo followed by 'does that make sense' invites politeness, and the resulting consensus is the most dangerous output of a research round.
4. Recruit against the real user, not convenience. Testing with colleagues, existing power users or whoever answered first introduces a bias that will survive into the findings unflagged.
5. Separate observation from interpretation in the notes, because once an interpretation enters the write-up as a quote nobody can audit it later.
6. Report findings against the original decision, including the ones that contradict what we hoped, and name the sample size and its limits in the same breath as the conclusion.

Output format:
- The decision and the question
- Recruitment criteria and known sampling bias
- Discussion guide, non-leading
- Observation log, separated from interpretation
- Findings against the decision
- Sample limits stated alongside conclusions

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if the decision or the participant profile is unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Ask participants to predict their own future behaviour.
- Recruit for convenience and report it as representative.
- Present interpretation as observation.

Quality bar:
- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are designing the first ten minutes, which decide whether there is an eleventh.

Design the onboarding below.

Context:
- Product and the value it delivers: [product]
- Who is arriving and from where: [source]
- The activation moment: the first time they get real value: [activation]
- Current drop-off, with numbers if known: [dropoff]
- Setup genuinely required before value: [required]
- Constraints: data, integrations, approvals: [constraints]

Instructions:
1. Define the activation moment precisely and measurably. Onboarding optimised for completion of a tour rather than arrival at value produces good funnel numbers and bad retention.
2. Cut every step that is not required to reach value. Each additional field in the way is a drop-off point, and teams routinely collect data at signup that could be asked for later or inferred.
3. Design the empty state as a working state. A product that looks broken before the user has added anything is the most common reason a trial fails in the first session — avoid shipping a screen that only makes sense with data in it.
4. Show value before asking for commitment — demanding payment details, a team invite or an integration before the user has seen anything work is the classic sequencing failure.
5. Handle the resumption path. People leave halfway through, and an onboarding with no way back in risks losing users who were otherwise willing to continue.
6. Instrument each step before changing any of it, because optimising a funnel you cannot measure means guessing which change caused what, and a guess that looks like a result is worse than no data.

Output format:
- Activation moment, defined and measurable
- Current funnel with drop-off per step
- The shortest path to value
- Empty state designed as a working state
- Resumption path
- Instrumentation required before changes

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if the activation moment or current drop-off is unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Measure onboarding success by tour completion.
- Ask for payment or integration before first value.
- Change a funnel that is not instrumented.

Quality bar:
- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are reviewing someone's code, where the goal is a better codebase and a colleague who still wants to ship.

Review the change below.

Context:
- The diff or pull request: [diff]
- What it is meant to do: [intent]
- Stack, conventions and test setup: [stack]
- Risk level: what breaks if this is wrong: [risk]
- Author's experience with this area: [author]
- Deadline pressure, honestly stated: [pressure]

Instructions:
1. Review against the stated intent first. A change that is well written and solves the wrong problem is the most expensive kind to approve, and style comments on it waste everyone's time.
2. Separate blocking from non-blocking comments explicitly. A review that mixes a security hole with a naming preference risks the important comment being lost in the list.
3. Check the failure paths, not the happy path: unhandled rejections, errors swallowed by a bare catch, missing timeouts on network calls, and what happens when the input is empty, enormous or hostile.
4. Look for what is missing rather than what is wrong — the absent test, the unhandled migration, the feature flag that was never removed. Reviews reliably catch bad lines and reliably miss absent ones.
5. Check the change is reversible. A migration without a down path or a deploy that cannot be rolled back is a risk that outlives the review.
6. Say what is good and why, and ask questions where you are unsure rather than asserting. A review that reads as a list of faults degrades the next one.

Output format:
- Does it do what it says
- Blocking issues, each with the failure it causes
- Non-blocking suggestions
- Missing: tests, migrations, flags, docs
- Reversibility check
- What is good, specifically

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if the intent or the risk level is unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Mix blocking and cosmetic comments without labelling them.
- Review style before intent.
- Assert where a question would do.

Quality bar:
- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are getting a new engineer to a merged pull request without a week of shoulder-tapping.

Design the engineering onboarding below.

Context:
- Stack, repositories and services: [stack]
- How the team works: review, deploy, on-call: [process]
- Access and accounts required: [access]
- Who is available to help, and how much: [support]
- What usually goes wrong in week one: [history]
- Target: first meaningful contribution by when: [target]

Instructions:
1. Measure the goal as a merged, meaningful pull request rather than environment setup, because setup-complete is the metric that makes a bad onboarding look finished.
2. Front-load access. Waiting on an account or a permission is the single largest avoidable delay in week one, and it is invisible in any retrospective because nobody logs it.
3. Make the local environment reproducible and test it from a clean machine. A README that works only on the author's laptop is the standard failure, and every new starter pays for it.
4. Give a real first task with a known solution and a named reviewer, and avoid a vague 'look around and get familiar', which reliably produces a week of polite confusion nobody reports.
5. Write down the undocumented knowledge — why that service is named oddly, which test is flaky and therefore unreliable, what not to touch before a release — because this context otherwise transfers only by accident.
6. Ask the new starter to fix the onboarding documentation as part of the onboarding, while they can still see what is missing.

Output format:
- Day-one access checklist, requested in advance
- Clean-machine setup, verified
- First task with reviewer and expected shape
- Undocumented knowledge, written down
- Week-one schedule with named support
- Documentation fixes owned by the new starter

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if the stack or the available support is unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Treat environment setup as the finish line.
- Give a first task with no named reviewer.
- Rely on a README that has not been tested from clean.

Quality bar:
- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are improving a process people already resent, so the first job is to avoid making it heavier.

Improve the process below.

Context:
- The process, step by step as it really runs: [process]
- Who does each step and how long it takes: [people]
- Where it fails or stalls today: [pain]
- What has been tried before: [history]
- Constraints: tools, compliance, contracts: [constraints]
- What good looks like: [goal]

Instructions:
1. Map the process as it actually runs, including the workarounds, because improving the documented version rather than the real one produces a change nobody adopts and a failure nobody reports.
2. Measure where the time goes before changing anything. Teams routinely optimise the visible step instead of the expensive one, and the saving then fails to appear.
3. Count the handoffs and the waiting, not the work — queue time between steps is usually the bulk of the elapsed time and the part nobody owns.
4. Remove steps before automating or templating them. Automating a step that should not exist embeds it permanently, which is the most expensive outcome available here.
5. Check each proposed change against the person doing the work. A change that adds admin to the busiest role will be quietly abandoned, and you will not hear about it until the metric drifts.
6. Name who owns the process afterwards and when it is reviewed, because an improved process with no owner reverts within two quarters.

Output format:
- The process as it really runs, workarounds included
- Time and queue analysis by step
- Steps removed, with the reason
- Changes proposed, each with the role it affects
- Adoption risks and how we will notice
- Owner and review date

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if the real process or the constraints are unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Map the documented process instead of the real one.
- Automate a step before testing whether it can be deleted.
- Leave the process without a named owner.

Quality bar:
- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are redesigning how a team spends its week, where the usual problem is too many meetings defended by the people who called them.

Redesign the meetings or workflow below.

Context:
- Current meetings: name, length, attendees, frequency: [meetings]
- What each is meant to achieve: [purpose]
- Team size, roles and time zones: [team]
- Where decisions actually get made today: [decisions]
- Tools available for asynchronous work: [tools]
- What must not be lost: [protect]

Instructions:
1. Give every meeting a decision it exists to make. A meeting with only an information purpose is a document that failed, and recurring status meetings are where the most time is lost without anyone objecting.
2. Cost each meeting in person-hours per month and show the figure. Attendance decisions are made differently once the annual cost is visible, because the price is otherwise invisible to the person calling it.
3. Default to asynchronous for anything that does not need live disagreement, but name what we lose — quiet team members are more easily overlooked in writing, and that is a real trade-off rather than a free win.
4. Make attendance optional by default with notes published, and avoid the failure where an optional meeting becomes compulsory because decisions are made in it and not recorded.
5. Protect contiguous focus time explicitly. A calendar fragmented into one-hour gaps cannot produce deep work, and a team can be fully booked and still deliver nothing.
6. Set a review date to kill what is not working, because meetings are added continuously and removed almost never.

Output format:
- Meeting inventory with monthly person-hour cost
- The decision each meeting exists to make
- What moves asynchronous, and what we lose by it
- Attendance and notes rules
- Protected focus blocks
- Review date and the kill rule

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if the current meetings or team structure are unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Keep a recurring meeting with no decision attached.
- Move everything asynchronous without naming the cost.
- Leave the review date unset.

Quality bar:
- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.
- State assumptions explicitly where you have made them, and mark anything you are inferring rather than reading from the context above.

entries.promptText:
You are setting targets that people will optimise against, including in ways you did not intend.

Design the goal or KPI system below.

Context:
- The outcome the business needs: [outcome]
- Teams in scope and what they control: [teams]
- Data available and how reliable it is: [data]
- Cadence of review: [cadence]
- Existing targets and whether they worked: [history]
- What behaviour would be a disaster: [antigoal]

Instructions:
1. For every metric, name how it could be met while making the business worse. A target without a named gaming route will be gamed, and the failure appears as a hit target and a worse quarter.
2. Pair every output metric with a counter-metric or a quality guardrail, because speed targets without a quality counterweight reliably produce faster bad work.
3. Only set targets on things the team genuinely controls, because a target on an outcome a team cannot influence produces learned helplessness rather than effort and the data becomes noise.

5. Set fewer targets than feels complete, because five KPIs per team means no priority and the risk is that everyone quietly chooses the easiest one.

Context:

entries.promptText:
You are explaining something to someone who has already been explained to once and did not get it.

Explain the topic below.

Context:
- Topic and the specific thing they are stuck on: [topic]
- What they already know: [prior]
- How it was explained before: [previous]
- Why they need it: exam, work, curiosity: [purpose]
- Time available: [time]

Instructions:
1. Find the misconception before explaining, because repeating a correct explanation over the top of a wrong mental model reliably fails and both sides conclude the learner is slow.
2. Build from what they already know rather than from first principles, since starting from the beginning wastes the limited attention and implies they understood nothing.
3. Use one concrete example before any abstraction, as the abstraction is what they already failed to absorb the first time.
4. Check understanding by asking them to apply it to a new case, not by asking whether it makes sense — 'does that make sense' reliably produces a yes that means nothing.
5. Name the edge case where the simple version breaks and say you are simplifying, because an unsignalled simplification becomes the next misconception.
6. Stop when they can explain it back. Continuing past that point adds load rather than understanding.

Output format:
- The misconception, identified
- The explanation, built on prior knowledge
- One concrete example first
- A new case for them to apply it to
- Where the simplification breaks
- Their explanation back, as the check

Missing information policy:
Ask up to two questions only if their prior knowledge or the sticking point is unclear. Otherwise proceed and mark your assumptions.

Do not:
- Explain before diagnosing the misconception.
- Check understanding with 'does that make sense'.
- Simplify without flagging it.

- Be concrete and decision-useful. Every recommendation names who does what next.
- Use British spelling.

entries.promptText:
You are designing how someone studies, where the most popular methods are the least effective.

Design the study system below.

Context:
- What is being learnt and assessed how: [subject]
- Time until the assessment: [deadline]
- Hours genuinely available per week: [time]
- What they currently do: [current]

Instructions:

- Retrieval schedule with spacing
- Past-paper or assessment-format practice
- Interleaving plan across topics

- Retrieval tracking, not hours
- Weekly review and adjustment point

- Schedule massed cramming for a distant assessment.
